隆慶改元之辛未復當會試
天下士屆期禮部尚書臣晟
侍郎臣希烈臣大綬以請
上若曰茲籲俊登獻惟重典其命
輔臣居正典試學士調陽輟

經術淺陋往荷
先帝簡拔侍
上於潛邸時時誦說所聞得效啓

經術淺陋徃荷
先帝簡拔侍
上於潛邸時時誦說所聞得效啓
沃及

punctuated:
會試錄序

隆慶改元之辛未，復當會試天下士。屆期，禮部尚書臣晟、侍郎臣希烈、臣大綬以請。上若曰：「茲籲俊登獻，惟重典。其命輔臣居正典試，學士調陽輟講筵事副之。」臣祗奉明命，不勝大幸。伏念臣一芥草茅，經術淺陋，往荷先帝簡拔，侍上於潛邸，時時誦說所聞，得效啓沃。及上登九五，錄用舊學，即召臣入賛機務，一歲中遷至孤卿，
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the xinwei year of the Longqing era [1571], it was again time to hold the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. When the appointed time arrived, your servant Sheng, Minister of Rites, and your servants Xilie and Dashou, Vice Ministers, submitted a request. His Majesty spoke thus: “Calling forth outstanding talent and advancing worthy men is a weighty institution. Let Grand Secretary Juzheng take charge of the examination, and let Academician Tiaoyang suspend his duties at the imperial lectures to assist him.” I reverently received this enlightened command, feeling myself fortunate beyond measure.

I humbly reflect that I was an insignificant man of humble origins, shallow and deficient in classical learning. Formerly, I was favored by the late emperor’s selection and served His present Majesty in his residence before his accession. From time to time I recited and explained what I had learned, thereby contributing to his instruction. When His Majesty ascended the imperial throne, he employed those who had formerly instructed him and immediately summoned me to assist in the central affairs of government. Within a single year I was promoted to Junior Guardian…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
夙夜兢兢念
皇上所以拔任臣者即捐糜一身
何足用報惟當蒐羅天下才
儁以布列周行共熈
帝載庶足以仰酬其萬一爾有告
臣曰某也賢克稱厥位輒手
記而心存之薦達之恐後某
===
===
也能克任厥職亦手記而心
存之薦達之恐後然負竒抱
藝伏在草莽者未有以聞也
乃今謬司校文之任得以盡
觀天下士簡汰而蒐拔之則
所知益廣所薦達益多而區
區圖報之忱亦可藉是以少
alt_text:
夙夜兢兢念
皇上所以拔任〔臣〕者即捐糜一身
何足用報惟當蒐羅天下才
儁以布列周行共熈
帝載庶足以仰酬其萬一爾有告
〔臣〕曰某也賢克稱厥位輙手
記而心存之薦達之恐後某
也能克任厥職亦手記而心
存之薦達之恐後然負奇抱
藝伏在草莽者未有以聞也
乃今謬司校文之任得以盡
觀天下士簡汰而蒐拔之則
所知益廣所薦達益多而區
區圖報之忱亦可藉是以少
punctuated: 夙夜兢兢，念皇上所以拔任臣者，即捐糜一身，何足用報？惟當蒐羅天下才儁，以布列周行，共熈帝載，庶足以仰酬其萬一爾。有告臣曰：「某也賢，克稱厥位。」輒手記而心存之，薦達之恐後。「某也能，克任厥職。」亦手記而心存之，薦達之恐後。然負竒抱藝，伏在草莽者，未有以聞也。乃今謬司校文之任，得以盡觀天下士，簡汰而蒐拔之，則所知益廣，所薦達益多，而區區圖報之忱，亦可藉是以少
translation_en: …Day and night I am apprehensive, reflecting on how Your Majesty has selected me for appointment. Even were I to sacrifice my life, how could that suffice to repay you? I can only seek out talented men throughout the realm and array them in the ranks of office, so that together they may advance the imperial enterprise. Perhaps this would repay one ten-thousandth of your favor. Whenever someone tells me, “So-and-so is worthy and well suited to his position,” I immediately make a note in my own hand and keep him in mind, fearing that I might be late in recommending him for advancement. When told, “So-and-so is capable and can discharge his duties,” I likewise make a note in my own hand and keep him in mind, fearing delay in recommending him. Yet I have had no means of learning about those who possess exceptional gifts and accomplishments but remain obscure outside official life. Now, undeservedly entrusted with the responsibility of assessing examination essays, I can survey the scholars of the entire realm, sift out the unworthy, and seek out and select the outstanding. Thus my knowledge of men will broaden and those whom I recommend will grow more numerous; through this, my humble, earnest desire to repay your favor may also to some degree…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
塞矣豈非臣之至幸至幸者
與乃以二月己亥偕臣調陽
及內外諸執事
陛辭入院合兩畿諸省前後所
貢士四千三百餘人如故事
三試之戒諸執事咸既乃心
試題必明白正大無或離析
===
章句以為竒異無或迎忌趨
好以長諛佞論文必崇尚雅
正無或眩華遺實以滋浮靡
有能綜覽古今直寫胷臆者
雖質弗棄非是者雖工弗錄
盖閱二旬而始竣遵
聖斷取四百人梓其姓名及其文

及內外諸執事

三試之戒諸執事咸旣乃心
識題必明白正大□□離析
===
章句以爲奇異無或□忌趨
好以長訣佞掄文必□尚雅
正無或眩華遺實以滋浮靡
有能綜覽古今直寫□臆者
雖質弗棄非是者雖工弗錄
蓋閱二旬而始竣事
□斷取四百人梓其姓名□其文
punctuated: 塞矣。豈非臣之至幸至幸者與？乃以二月己亥，偕臣調陽及內外諸執事陛辭入院，合兩畿諸省前後所貢士四千三百餘人，如故事三試之。戒諸執事咸既乃心：試題必明白正大，無或離析章句以為竒異，無或迎忌趨好以長諛佞；論文必崇尚雅正，無或眩華遺實以滋浮靡。有能綜覽古今、直寫胷臆者，雖質弗棄；非是者，雖工弗錄。盖閱二旬而始竣，遵聖斷取四百人，梓其姓名及其文
translation_en:
…may thus be fulfilled in some small measure. Is this not your servant’s greatest good fortune, his greatest good fortune indeed? Accordingly, on the jihai day of the second month, together with your servant Diaoyang and all the officials serving inside and outside the examination compound, I took leave of Your Majesty and entered the compound. We assembled the more than 4,300 candidates recommended over successive occasions by the two metropolitan regions and the provinces and, following precedent, examined them in three sessions.

I admonished all the officials to devote themselves wholeheartedly to their duties: examination questions must be clear, straightforward, upright, and proper. They must not break apart chapters and sentences to contrive peculiarities, nor cater to aversions and preferences so as to encourage flattery. In judging essays, they must esteem refinement and correctness, neither being dazzled by ornament nor neglecting substance, thereby encouraging superficial extravagance. Those able to survey past and present comprehensively and express their thoughts directly were not to be rejected even if their writing was plain; those who failed in these respects were not to be selected, however polished their writing.

Only after some twenty days was the work completed. In accordance with Your Majesty’s decision, we selected four hundred men and had their names and their writings cut into printing blocks…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
之優者焉録以
獻録既成臣與臣調陽暨諸執
事聚而觀之曰文不近實矣
乎僉曰實矣士能盡如其文
矣乎曰未可知也雖然既以
是取之敢不以是望之顧諸
士脫蒯屨而登
===
===
王庭猶未知
上意之所嚮與已之所趨者宜何
如也臣請告之以定厥志臣
聞世之治也恒自文而返質
其既也恒自質而之文昔者
孔子欲損周之文從夏之忠
而不可得有能究禮之本者
alt_text:
之優者爲録以
獻録既成〔臣〕顒〔臣〕訓暘暨諸執
事聚而觀之曰文不近實矣
乎僉曰實矣士能盡如其文
矣乎曰未可知也雖然既以
是取之敢不以是望之顧諸
士脫繭屣而登
===
王庭猶未知
上意之所嚮與已之所趨者宜何
如也〔臣〕請告之以定厥志〔臣〕
聞世之治也恒自文而返質
其既也恒自質而之文昔者
孔子欲損周之文從夏之忠
而不可得有能究禮之本者
punctuated:
之優者焉，録以獻。録既成，臣與臣調陽暨諸執事聚而觀之，曰：「文不近實矣乎？」僉曰：「實矣。」「士能盡如其文矣乎？」曰：「未可知也。雖然，既以是取之，敢不以是望之？顧諸士脫蒯屨而登王庭，猶未知上意之所嚮與已之所趨者宜何如也。臣請告之，以定厥志。」
臣聞世之治也，恒自文而返質；其既也，恒自質而之文。昔者孔子欲損周之文，從夏之忠，而不可得。有能究禮之本者，
translation_en:
…the finest of their writings, compiling them into a record for presentation to the throne. Once the record was completed, your servant, together with your servant Diaoyang and the officials responsible, gathered to examine it. I said, “Do these writings not approach substance?” All replied, “They do.” “Can these scholars fully live up to their writings?” The reply was, “That cannot yet be known.” “Nevertheless, since we have selected them on this basis, dare we fail to expect this of them? Yet these scholars, casting off their rush sandals to enter the royal court, still do not know the direction of His Majesty’s intentions or what course they themselves ought to pursue. Allow your servant to explain this to them, so as to settle their resolve.”
Your servant has heard that, when the world is well governed, it invariably returns from refinement to substance; afterward, it invariably moves from substance toward refinement. In former times, Confucius wished to temper the refinement of the Zhou and follow the sincerity of the Xia, but could not achieve this. Whenever someone could fathom the root of ritual…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
則深嘉而亟歎之誠達於時
宜如此也
明興二百餘年俗凡幾變矣我
皇上嗣大歷服於茲五年懸象布
令作則垂範一切務剽剥枝
蔓以崇本質省章奏之繁詞
握黙運之元柄言不蘄工期盡誠
===
款行不蘄卓取裨實用
側席寤寐惟欲得忠信誠愨直諒
不欺之士而任之故臣敢以
諸士進夫帝有帝臣王有王
佐霸有霸偶
今上所修帝道也諸士固且願爲
帝臣其尚一乃心端乃志毋作僞
alt_text:
則深嘉而亟歎之誠逴於時
宜如此也
明興二百餘年俗凡幾變矣我
皇上嗣大歷服於茲五年懸象布
令作則垂範一切務剷剝枝
蔓以崇本質省章奏之繁詞
握默運之元柄言不斵工期盡誠
===
欵行不斵卓取裨實用
側席寤寐惟欲得忠信誠慤直諒
不欺之士而任之故臣敢以
諸士進夫帝有帝臣王有王
佐霸有霸偶
今上所修帝道也諸士固且願爲
帝臣其尚一乃心端乃志毋作偽
punctuated:
則深嘉而亟歎之，誠達於時宜如此也。
明興二百餘年，俗凡幾變矣。我皇上嗣大歷服，於茲五年，懸象布令，作則垂範，一切務剽剥枝蔓，以崇本質。省章奏之繁詞，握黙運之元柄，言不蘄工，期盡誠款；行不蘄卓，取裨實用。側席寤寐，惟欲得忠信誠愨、直諒不欺之士而任之，故臣敢以諸士進。夫帝有帝臣，王有王佐，霸有霸偶。今上所修，帝道也。諸士固且願爲帝臣，其尚一乃心，端乃志，毋作僞
translation_en:
…then he praised them deeply and repeatedly expressed his admiration. Such indeed was his understanding of what suited the times.
More than two hundred years have passed since the Ming arose; how many changes have popular customs undergone! It is now five years since Our Emperor succeeded to the great imperial mandate [?]. He has displayed models and promulgated commands, established standards and set examples. In everything, he strives to strip away tangled branches so as to honor the essential substance. He reduces the verbose language of memorials and holds the supreme authority that works silently. In speech, he seeks no elegance, but expects the fullest sincerity; in conduct, he seeks no extraordinary distinction, but values contributions to practical use. He sits with a place beside him left vacant for worthy men; waking and sleeping, his sole desire is to obtain men who are loyal, trustworthy, sincere, honest, upright, and free from deceit, and to entrust them with office. Thus your servant ventures to recommend these gentlemen.
An emperor has an emperor’s ministers; a king has a king’s assistants; a hegemon has a hegemon’s partners. What His Present Majesty cultivates is the Way of the emperors. You gentlemen surely aspire to become ministers worthy of an emperor. May you therefore make your hearts single-minded and your purposes upright, and practice no falsehood…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
以亂真毋矜名以示異毋窾
言而不中其實毋詭故而不
近人情寧拙而遲毋巧而速
寧有瑕而爲玉毋似瑜而爲
石忠信質直以事其
上若是斯可以爲
帝臣而無負於今日之舉矣不然
是
主與臣意異矣臣
主異意不能治三家况天下乎臣
事
皇上久竊有以闚
上意之所在故於諸士始進之日
而告之以此夫士有才而不

===
主與臣意異矣臣
是
主異意不能治三家況天下乎臣
事
皇上久竊有以闚
上意之所在故於諸士始進之日
而告之以此夫士有才而不
punctuated: 以亂真，毋矜名以示異，毋窾言而不中其實，毋詭故而不近人情。寧拙而遲，毋巧而速；寧有瑕而爲玉，毋似瑜而爲石。忠信質直，以事其上。若是，斯可以爲帝臣，而無負於今日之舉矣。不然，是主與臣意異矣。臣主異意，不能治三家，况天下乎？臣事皇上久，竊有以闚上意之所在，故於諸士始進之日而告之以此。夫士有才而不
translation_en: …to confound the genuine. Do not vaunt your reputation to appear exceptional; do not utter empty words that fail to accord with the facts; do not resort to strange contrivances at odds with human feeling. Better to be clumsy and slow than clever and swift; better to be jade with flaws than stone resembling fine jade. Serve your sovereign with loyalty, trustworthiness, sincerity, and uprightness. Thus you may become ministers worthy of an emperor and not betray the purpose of your selection today. Otherwise, sovereign and ministers will differ in their intentions. When ministers and sovereign differ in their intentions, they cannot govern even three households—how much less All Under Heaven! Your servant has long served Your Majesty and ventures to think he has gained some insight into Your Majesty’s intentions. Therefore, on this day when you gentlemen first advance toward office, I offer you these words. Now, if a scholar possesses talent but is not…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
以進有司之過也
主德不宣申令不熟標準不立約
束不明臣等之過也
主德已宣申令已熟而眾弗率則
士之過也若是者謂之躍冶
之金匠者睨而棄之邦有常
刑臣不敢庇於戲登茲錄者
===
可不勗哉可不懼哉是役也
同考試官則中允臣時行臣
錫爵修撰臣萬化編修臣棟
臣洛文臣志皐臣家屏臣維
楨檢討臣國臣鯉臣思育都
給事中臣楫臣良佐右給事
中臣樹德郎中臣藿臣三接
alt_text:
以進有司之過也
主德不宣申令不熟標準不立約
束不明臣等之過也
主德已宣申令已熟而衆弗率則
士之過也若是者謂之曜治
之金匠者睨而棄之邦有常
刑臣不敢庇於戲登茲籙者
可不勗哉可不懼哉是役也
===
同考試官則中允臣時行臣
錫爵修撰臣萬化編修臣棟
臣洛文臣志皐臣家屛臣維
楨檢討臣國臣鯉臣思育都
給事中臣楫臣良佐右給事
中臣樹德郎中臣藿臣三接
punctuated:
以進，有司之過也。主德不宣，申令不熟，標準不立，約束不明，臣等之過也。主德已宣，申令已熟，而眾弗率，則士之過也。若是者，謂之躍冶之金，匠者睨而棄之。邦有常刑，臣不敢庇。於戲！登茲錄者，可不勗哉？可不懼哉？
是役也，同考試官則中允臣時行、臣錫爵，修撰臣萬化，編修臣棟、臣洛文、臣志皐、臣家屏、臣維楨，檢討臣國、臣鯉、臣思育，都給事中臣楫、臣良佐，右給事中臣樹德，郎中臣藿、臣三接
translation_en:
…are advanced on that basis, the fault lies with the responsible officials. If the ruler’s virtue is not made known, his reiterated commands are not thoroughly understood, standards are not established, and regulations are not clear, the fault lies with us, your servants. If the ruler’s virtue has been made known and his reiterated commands thoroughly understood, yet the candidates fail to comply, then the fault lies with the candidates. Such men are called metal that leaps from the casting furnace: the craftsman glances at it and casts it aside. The state has its established punishments; I, your servant, dare not shield them. Alas! Can those whose names appear in this record fail to exert themselves? Can they fail to feel apprehension?
For this examination, the Associate Examiners were your servants Shixing and Xijue, Vice Mentors; Wanhua, Senior Compiler; Dong, Luowen, Zhigao, Jiaping, and Weizhen, Junior Compilers; Guo, Li, and Siyu, Examining Editors; Ji and Liangzuo, Chief Supervising Secretaries; Shude, Right Supervising Secretary; and Huo and Sanjie, Bureau Directors…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
臣緝監試則御史臣標臣友
賢寔相與成事而御史臣洤
道明臣侯居艮則防檢於外
者例得並書云
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
建極殿大學士張居正謹序
alt_text:
臣絹監試則御史〔臣標臣友〕
賢寔相與成事而御史〔臣吳〕
道明〔臣侯居艮〕則防檢於外
者例得並書云
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
建極殿大學士張〔居正〕謹序
punctuated:
臣緝。監試則御史臣標、臣友賢，寔相與成事。而御史臣洤道明、臣侯居艮，則防檢於外者，例得並書云。
光祿大夫、柱國、少傅兼太子太傅、吏部尚書、建極殿大學士張居正謹序。
translation_en:
…and your servant Ji. The examination monitors were the Censors, your servants Biao and Youxian, who indeed worked together to bring this undertaking to completion. The Censors, your servants Quan Daoming [?] and Hou Jugen, were responsible for guarding and inspecting outside; by established practice, their names are also recorded here.
Respectfully prefaced by Zhang Juzheng, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Jianji Hall.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Fifth Year of Longqing (1571).

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Pan Sheng, Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Siming and was from Xinchang County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinchou year (1541).

Wang Xilie, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Zizhong. Registered in Nanchang County, Jiangxi, and originally from Linchuan County, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Examiners

Zhang Juzheng held the titles Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor, concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Establishing the Pole. His courtesy name was Shuda; he was from Jingzhou Guard, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Lü Diaoyang, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy and in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, had the courtesy name Heqing. Registered in Guilin Central Guard, Guangxi, and originally from Daye County, Huguang, he became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Associate Examiners

Shen Shixing, Left Assistant Director of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently a Hanlin Academy Editor, had the courtesy name Rumo. Registered in Wu County, Zhili, and originally from Changzhou County, he became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1562).

Wang Xijue, Right Assistant Director of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently a Hanlin Academy Editor, had the courtesy name Yuanyu. He was from Taicang Subprefecture, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1562).

Luo Wanhua, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler and Gentleman for Attending to Affairs, had the courtesy name Yifu. He was from Kuaiji County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1568).

Chen Dong, Hanlin Academy Editor and Gentleman of the Forest of Literature, had the courtesy name Longzhi. Registered in Jinxian County, Jiangxi, and originally from Nanchang County, he became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1565).

He Luowen, Hanlin Academy Editor and Gentleman of the Forest of Literature, had the courtesy name Qitu. He was from Xinyang Subprefecture, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1565).

Zhao Zhigao, Hanlin Academy Editor and Gentleman for Rendering Service, had the courtesy name Rumai. He was from Lanxi County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1568).

Wang Jiaping, Hanlin Academy Editor and Gentleman for Rendering Service, had the courtesy name Zhongbo. He was from Shanyin County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1568).

Li Weizhen, Hanlin Academy Editor and Gentleman for Rendering Service, had the courtesy name Benning. He was from Jingshan County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1568).

Xu Guo, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler and Gentleman for Meritorious Service, had the courtesy name Weizhen. He was from She County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1565).

Shen Li, Hanlin Academy Junior Compiler and Gentleman for Meritorious Service, had the courtesy name Zhonghua. Registered in Guide Guard, Henan, and originally from Kunshan County, Zhili, he became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1565).

Chen Siyu, Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, held the prestige title Gentleman for Distinguished Service. His courtesy name was Renfu; he was from Wuling County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1565 (yichou).

Han Ji, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel, had the courtesy name Botong. He was registered in the Puzhou Guard Battalion, Shanxi, and was a native of Yangzhou, Zhili; he became a metropolitan graduate in 1565 (yichou).

Song Liangzuo, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, had the courtesy name Shouzhong. He was from Wanzai County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1565 (yichou).

Lu Shude, Right Vice Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for War, had the courtesy name Yucheng. He was from Huating County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1565 (yichou).

Lü Huo, Director of the Bureau of Evaluations in the Ministry of Personnel, held the prestige title Grand Master for Administrative Service. His courtesy name was Chenqing; he was from Lingling County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1562 (renxu).

Yuan Sanjie, Secretary acting as Director of the Yunnan Bureau in the Ministry of Revenue, held the prestige title Gentleman for Attending to Virtue. His courtesy name was Bangjiao; he was from Xiangshan County, Guangdong, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1562 (renxu).

Wang Ji, Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Operations in the Ministry of War, held the prestige title Gentleman for Attending to Virtue. His courtesy name was Xifu; he was registered in Fenzhou, Shanxi, and was a native of Dingyuan County, Zhili. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1559 (jiwei).

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Yang Biao, Investigating Censor for the Huguang Circuit, held the prestige title Gentleman of Literary Service. His courtesy name was Tingzhan; he was from Qingjiang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1556 (bingchen).

Wang Youxian, Investigating Censor for the Huguang Circuit, held the prestige title Gentleman of Literary Service. His courtesy name was Xiyao; he was from Ningxiang County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1559 (jiwei).

Proctors:

Li Fengyang, Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige title Gentleman for Upright Service. His courtesy name was Weiming; he was from the Jinwu Rear Guard in Nanjing and became a metropolitan graduate in 1568 (wuchen).

Liu Yingqi, Secretary of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige title Gentleman for Upright Service. His courtesy name was Daozheng; he was from Poyang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1568 (wuchen).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Lu Guangzuo, Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige title Gentleman for Attending to Virtue. His courtesy name was Yupei; he was from Pinghu County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1559 (jiwei).

Tao Yunchun, Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige title Gentleman for Upright Service. His courtesy name was Maochu; he was from Kuaiji County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1565 (yichou).

Officials Responsible for the Custody of Examination Scripts:

Zhang Yuanxiao, Secretary of the Bureau of Imperial Entertainments in the Ministry of Rites, performing the duties of a Central Secretariat Drafter, held the prestige title Gentleman for Attending to Virtue. His courtesy name was Tianjing; he was from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and was an official student (guansheng).

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
生財有大道生之者衆食之者寡爲之者
疾用之者舒則財恒足矣
子曰先進於禮樂野人也後進於禮樂君
子也如用之則吾從先進
有安社稷臣者以安社稷爲悅者也有天
民者達可行於天下而後行之者也有
大人者正己而物正者也
===
易
文言曰元者善之長也亨者嘉之會也利
者義之和也貞者事之幹也君子體仁
足以長人嘉會足以合禮利物足以和
義貞固足以幹事君子行此四德者故
曰乾元亨利貞
重巽以申命
以制器者尚其象
有大者不可以盈故受之以謙有大而能

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

生財有大道：生之者衆，食之者寡，爲之者疾，用之者舒，則財恒足矣。

子曰：「先進於禮樂，野人也；後進於禮樂，君子也。如用之，則吾從先進。」

有安社稷臣者，以安社稷爲悅者也；有天民者，達可行於天下而後行之者也；有大人者，正己而物正者也。

易

文言曰：「元者，善之長也；亨者，嘉之會也；利者，義之和也；貞者，事之幹也。君子體仁，足以長人；嘉會，足以合禮；利物，足以和義；貞固，足以幹事。君子行此四德者，故曰：『乾，元亨利貞。』」

重巽以申命。

以制器者尚其象。

有大者不可以盈，故受之以謙；有大而能
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

There is a great way to produce wealth: let those who produce it be many and those who consume it few; let those who make it be diligent and those who use it be sparing. Then wealth will always be sufficient.

The Master said: “Those of earlier times who practiced rites and music were regarded as rustic people; those of later times who practiced rites and music were regarded as gentlemen. If I were to employ these practices, I would follow those of earlier times.”

There are ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain, taking pleasure in securing the state. There are Heaven’s people, who act only after attaining a position in which their Way can be put into practice throughout the world. There are great men, who rectify themselves and thereby set other things right.

Book of Changes

The Commentary on the Words says: “The primal is the chief of all goodness; success is the convergence of all that is excellent; benefit is the harmony of righteousness; constancy is the mainstay of affairs. By embodying benevolence, the gentleman is able to lead others; by bringing together what is excellent, he is able to accord with ritual propriety; by benefiting things, he is able to harmonize righteousness; by remaining constant and firm, he is able to manage affairs. The gentleman practices these four virtues. Thus it is said: ‘Qian: primality, success, benefit, and constancy.’”

Xun doubled: thereby to reiterate commands.

Those who use it to fashion implements prize its images.

Those who possess greatness must not become full of themselves; therefore it is followed by Qian, Modesty. Possessing greatness and being able to…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
謙必豫故受之以豫
書
皐陶曰都在知人在安民禹曰吁咸若時
惟帝其難之知人則哲能官人安民則
惠黎民懷之
啓乃心沃朕心
自朝至于日中昃不遑暇食用咸和萬民
爾身克正罔敢弗正民心罔中惟爾之中
詩
===
如切如磋如琢如磨瑟兮僩兮赫兮咺兮
旣見君子德音孔膠心乎愛矣遐不謂矣
中心藏之何日忘之
小心翼翼昭事上帝
自彼氐羌莫敢不來享莫敢不來王曰商
是常
春秋
秋齊侯宋公江人黃人會于陽穀〔僖公三年〕
春王正月公會齊侯宋公陳侯衞侯

punctuated:
謙，必豫，故受之以豫。

書
皐陶曰：「都！在知人，在安民。」禹曰：「吁！咸若時，惟帝其難之。知人則哲，能官人；安民則惠，黎民懷之。」
啓乃心，沃朕心。
自朝至于日中昃，不遑暇食，用咸和萬民。
爾身克正，罔敢弗正；民心罔中，惟爾之中。

詩
如切如磋，如琢如磨。瑟兮僩兮，赫兮咺兮。
旣見君子，德音孔膠。心乎愛矣，遐不謂矣？
中心藏之，何日忘之？
小心翼翼，昭事上帝。
自彼氐羌，莫敢不來享，莫敢不來王，曰商是常。

春秋
秋，齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人會于陽穀。〔僖公三年〕
春，王正月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衞侯
translation_en:
…modest, there must be joy; therefore it is followed by Yu (Joy).

Book of Documents
Gao Yao said: “Ah! It lies in knowing people and bringing peace to the people.” Yu said: “Ah! To accomplish all this—even the emperor would find it difficult. Knowing people is wisdom: one can appoint people to office. Bringing peace to the people is benevolence: the common people cherish such a ruler.”
Open your heart and refresh my heart.
From dawn until the sun had passed its zenith, he had no leisure to eat; thus he brought all the myriad people into harmony.
If your own person is upright, none will dare to be otherwise. The people's hearts have no fixed mean; they take your mean as their own.

Book of Odes
As though cut and filed, as though carved and polished. How solemn and dignified! How radiant and distinguished!
Having seen the noble man, I find his virtuous words bind us firmly together. In my heart I love him; why should I not tell him?
I treasure him in my heart; on what day could I forget him?
With reverent care, he illustriously served the Lord on High.
Even from among those Di and Qiang, none dared fail to come to present offerings; none dared fail to come to acknowledge the king, saying: “This is the constant rule of Shang.”

Question: The explanation of the Tai hexagram in the Book of Changes says: “Heaven and earth interact, and the myriad things flourish; those above and those below interact, and their intentions are united.” Thus, what is meant by Tai—peace and prosperity—surely lies in the relationship between ruler and ministers. In a time of Tai, harmonious influences pervade all, and good government flourishes. If there is any obstruction, it cannot qualify as Tai. By what means did the enlightened rulers and worthy ministers of old work together first to establish such peace and prosperity and then to preserve it? Since antiquity, a felicitous meeting between ruler and ministers has been considered difficult to achieve; how, then, did they establish this mutual intercourse?

The ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and the Three Dynasties are remote indeed. From the Han onward, there were those who discussed the principles of government and did not retire until midnight; those who decreed that remonstrance officials should accompany the chief ministers when they entered to deliberate on affairs of state; those who issued personally written edicts and supplied brushes and writing materials; and those who requested that attendant officials take turns remaining on duty overnight to await an imperial summons. Did these not also approach what is meant by peace and prosperity through mutual intercourse?

…the Two Founders; for preserving peaceful prosperity, none surpassed the reigns of Xuanzong and Xiaozong. Could one enumerate all the counselors, strategists, venerable veterans, and mature statesmen who attended them in their inner councils, deliberated on affairs of state, and helped bring about peace? The procedures for court lectures were already fully set forth in the statutes, yet they also summoned officials at irregular intervals. Was this not troublesome and taxing? Since Our Emperor ascended the throne, he has pursued learning and diligently attended to government, gladly joining all his officials in attaining peaceful rule. His profound beneficence and awe-inspiring commands have brought even the distant wilderness into order. This, too, is evidence of the peaceful prosperity that comes from communication between ruler and ministers. Yet the ancients said: “On a journey of a hundred li, reckon ninety as only halfway.” When on level ground, to remain mindful of slopes; when things depart, to consider their return—this is the crux of preserving peaceful prosperity. Please elaborate on these ideas to help preserve peaceful prosperity today.

…were defective laws under previous dynasties, yet are sound institutions under our illustrious dynasty: might there indeed be a proper way to implement them? Nevertheless, by now they too are becoming defective. Should they be reformed or not? Some say the trouble lies simply in a failure to conduct comprehensive scrutiny. Among rulers past and present discussed in connection with comprehensive scrutiny, none compares with Emperor Xuan of the Han. Yet in his time, official business was attended to only once every five days; officials failed to promulgate imperial edicts; those submitting annual accounting registers supplied mere formalities; and those who fraudulently inflated the registers received rewards. Can this be called enforcing the laws? Is the judgment that Xuan surpassed Emperor Wen a sound general conclusion? Why do some express such urgent admiration for him? Furthermore, Xuan’s praise of Yuan [?] seems to indicate an understanding of the essentials, yet some sharply condemn it as wrong. Which judgment is correct? If one wishes to conduct comprehensive scrutiny, the true circumstances and the deceptions cannot all be fathomed; if one undertakes reform, there are sound institutions that need not be changed. Truly, it is difficult to know which course to follow. Consider carefully what would be advantageous and set it down in your essay.

豪傑未必聖賢聖賢必為豪傑而古惟

translation_en:
…recorded in the histories are too numerous to enumerate. Yet some were expressly given such designations as the Four Outstanding Men of Shu, the Seven Mighty Men of Zhou, the Four Eminent Men of the Warring States, and the Three Worthies of Han. Did their talents, conduct, reputations, and achievements truly all merit these names? Or were there differences of higher and lower quality among them? Recent Confucian scholars say that true heroes must emerge from fearful vigilance. They also say that eminent men need not be sages or worthies, but sages and worthies must be eminent men, and that in antiquity only three sages fully deserved this designation. Are these claims not even more remarkable? “Hero” and “eminent man” are fine names; for a scholar to earn such a designation may well be considered difficult. Yet Confucian scholars still criticize them, allowing them little indulgence. Whom, then, should those who seek fellowship with the ancients take as their models? Explain this, so that we may discern your aspirations.
Question: Only by knowing men can one appoint them to office; this has been considered difficult since antiquity. Under Yao and Shun, appointments were considered according to the nine virtues; the Zhou assessed officials according to the six accomplishments. This surely reflected their care. Confucian scholars delight in discussing past and present and appraising individuals, producing a profusion of opinions. Ban Gu’s Table of Persons Past and Present gathers individuals from several thousand years and ranks them through critical assessment. How detailed it is in its arrangement into nine grades and its categories of sages, the benevolent, the wise, and the foolish! But do the broad distinctions in human talents and dispositions extend only this far? Liu Shao’s Treatise on Personalities (Renwu zhi) identifies twelve types of professional endeavor, assigning corresponding duties and responsibilities to each. His account is most impressive. In regard to appointing officials, did he …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
之大法固有見歟乃張晏李德裕之徒
猶詆訾之何也豈拘儒臆說無關于知
人之術歟抑知人寔難儒者不能殫其
說歟今
國家取賢斂才采名責實科條非益簡而議
論非寡也乃海內有急率稱乏材何歟
議者謂宜廣登籲之途明器使之道公
久任之法覈功效之實然歟否歟夫需
材甚亟而理效則疎論人愈嚴而致用
===

究言之俟用人者采焉
問古今言制禦夷狄者不出乎戰守和三
策矣試以漢事言之和親遣使中國之

而或又以為勞然則三策果孰善歟賈
誼憤匈奴之桀驁請為屬國以制之其

之大法固有見歟？乃張晏、李德裕之徒猶詆訾之，何也？豈拘儒臆說，無關于知人之術歟？抑知人寔難，儒者不能殫其說歟？今國家取賢斂才，采名責實，科條非益簡，而議論非寡也。乃海內有急，率稱乏材，何歟？議者謂宜廣登籲之途，明器使之道，公久任之法，覈功效之實，然歟？否歟？夫需材甚亟，而理效則疎；論人愈嚴，而致用則匱。轉移鼓舞之術，將安出也？諸士試究言之，俟用人者采焉。

問：古今言制禦夷狄者，不出乎戰、守、和三策矣。試以漢事言之：和親遣使，中國之利也，而或又以為辱；幕南空庭，武功盛矣，而或又以為黷；朔方繕塞，設險固矣，而或又以為勞。然則三策果孰善歟？賈誼憤匈奴之桀驁，請為屬國以制之，其志壯矣，而所謂三表五餌者，乃更出於
translation_en:
…did he indeed have insight into the great principles of appointing officials? Why, then, did men such as Zhang Yan and Li Deyu nevertheless disparage him? Were these merely the conjectures of a hidebound scholar, irrelevant to the art of judging men? Or is judging men truly so difficult that scholars cannot fully explain it? Today the state selects the worthy and gathers talent, considers reputations and demands actual achievement. Its regulations have hardly become simpler, nor has discussion been scant. Yet whenever an emergency arises within the realm, people invariably complain of a shortage of talent. Why is this? Some argue that we should broaden the avenues for summoning and promoting men, clarify how to employ them according to their abilities, administer impartially the rules for keeping them long in office, and scrutinize their actual accomplishments. Is this right or not? The need for talent is urgent, yet the results of government are meager; judgments of men grow ever stricter, yet men available for practical service are lacking. What means can be found to bring about change and inspire them? You candidates should examine these matters and explain them fully, so that those responsible for employing men may draw upon your views.

Question: From antiquity to the present, discussions of controlling and defending against the non-Chinese peoples have never gone beyond three policies: war, defense, and peace. Consider the affairs of the Han. Marriage alliances and the dispatch of envoys benefited the central realm, yet some considered them humiliating. The enemy’s encampments south of the desert were emptied—a splendid military achievement—yet some considered this an excessive resort to arms. Frontier fortifications were repaired in Shuofang, making the defenses strong, yet some considered this an exhausting burden. Which of these three policies, then, is truly best? Indignant at the defiance of the Xiongnu, Jia Yi requested appointment as Director of Dependent States to bring them under control. His ambition was indeed grand, yet his so-called “three demonstrations and five baits” ranked even below…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
歲繒之下何歟當時名臣畫士如仲舒
安國魏相望之之流皆嘗風議於帷幄
爭辯於廟堂矣而其論各不相下乃陸
氏又謂古今異宜彊弱異勢要在隨時
觀變毋執一議者然歟否歟虜爲邊患
久矣乃今忽欵塞乞封斯寔
朝廷威德所及比之前代和議固不侔矣然
外寧內憂聖人所戒可遂忘戰罷守不
講歟斬渾邪以謝百姓激言也而當時
===
韙之罷邊備以休吏卒便計也而議者
非之其言孰當歟法曰無恃其不來恃
吾有以待之今吾所以待虜者果皆備
歟制御之策安所出歟諸士懷當世之
慮久矣其極言之毋有所諱

歲縉之下何與當時名臣叢士如仲淹
安國魏相望之之流皆嘗風議於帷幄
爭辯於廟堂矣而其論各不相下乃臣
氏又謂古今異宜彊弱異勢要在隨時
觀變毋執一議者然歟否歟虜爲邊患

外寇内憂聖人所戒可遂忘戰罷守不
講歟斬渾邪以謝百姓激言也而當時
===
雖之罷邊備以休吏卒便計也而議者
非之其言孰當歟法曰無恃其不來恃
吾有以待之今吾所以待虜者果皆備
歟制御之策安所出歟諸士懷當世之
慮久矣其極言之毋有所諱
punctuated: 歲繒之下，何歟？當時名臣畫士，如仲舒、安國、魏相、望之之流，皆嘗風議於帷幄，爭辯於廟堂矣，而其論各不相下。乃陸氏又謂古今異宜，彊弱異勢，要在隨時觀變，毋執一議者，然歟否歟？虜爲邊患久矣，乃今忽欵塞乞封，斯寔朝廷威德所及，比之前代和議，固不侔矣。然外寧內憂，聖人所戒，可遂忘戰罷守，不講歟？斬渾邪以謝百姓，激言也，而當時韙之；罷邊備以休吏卒，便計也，而議者非之。其言孰當歟？法曰：「無恃其不來，恃吾有以待之。」今吾所以待虜者，果皆備歟？制御之策，安所出歟？諸士懷當世之慮久矣，其極言之，毋有所諱。
translation_en:
…inferior even to the annual tribute of silk—why was this? Distinguished ministers and strategists of that time, such as Zhongshu, Anguo, Wei Xiang, and Wangzhi, all offered counsel in the imperial council and debated at court, yet none would yield to the others in their arguments. Master Lu, however, held that what is appropriate differs between ancient and modern times, and that circumstances differ according to relative strength and weakness: the essential thing is to observe changes as they occur and not cling to a single proposal. Is this correct or not?

The barbarians have long troubled the frontier. Now, suddenly, they have approached our border fortifications and requested enfeoffment. This is indeed the effect of the court’s might and virtue, and certainly cannot be equated with the peace negotiations of previous dynasties. Yet outward tranquility accompanied by internal troubles is something against which the sage warned. Can we therefore forget warfare, abandon defense, and cease considering these matters? To execute Hunye in order to make amends to the common people was an extreme proposal, yet contemporaries approved it; to discontinue frontier defenses in order to give officials and soldiers respite was an expedient plan, yet commentators condemned it. Which view was right?

The military text says: “Do not rely on their not coming; rely on our having the means to meet them.” Are all our means of meeting the barbarians now truly in readiness? From where should a strategy for controlling them come? You candidates have long pondered the concerns of the present age. Set forth your views fully, withholding nothing.

親切盖嘗留心治道者

第壹場
四書
「生財有大道：生之者衆，食之者寡，為之者疾，用之者舒，則財恒足矣。」
鄧以讚
同考試官檢討沈批：「經國大計，具見此文。」
同考試官檢討許批：「理財要務，不出此數言矣。佳士！佳士！」
同考試官編修李批：「體格平正，詞意醇雅。」
同考試官編修王批：「務本節用，生財至計，此作發明親切，盖嘗留心治道者。」
同考試官編修陳批：「大雅之文，可式多士。」
考試官學士吕批：「理財大道，發揮透徹。」
考試官大學士張批：「篇末歸重節儉，是識時務者。」
善理財者，得其道而自裕焉。盖務本節用，生財之道也。果能此道矣，國孰與不足乎？且夫聚人曰財，國而無財，非其國矣；理財曰義，財而不義，非其財矣。是以君子之生財也有道焉，固不必
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“There is a great way to produce wealth: let those who produce it be many, those who consume it few, those who work at it diligent, and those who spend it restrained; then wealth will always be sufficient.”
Deng Yizan
Associate Examiner Shen, an Examining Editor, comments: “The great plans for governing a state are fully evident in this essay.”
Associate Examiner Xu, an Examining Editor, comments: “The essential tasks of managing wealth do not go beyond these few words. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!”
Associate Examiner Li, a Compiler, comments: “Its form is balanced and correct; its language and ideas are refined and elegant.”
Associate Examiner Wang, a Compiler, comments: “Attending to the root—agriculture—and restraining expenditure are the best plans for producing wealth. This essay elucidates them aptly and directly. Its author must have given thought to the way of governing.”
Associate Examiner Chen, a Compiler, comments: “An essay of great elegance, fit to serve as a model for the many scholars.”
Examiner Lü, an Academician, comments: “The great way of managing wealth is expounded thoroughly.”
Examiner Zhang, a Grand Secretary, comments: “The essay ends by placing the chief emphasis on frugality. Here is someone who understands the needs of the times.”
Those skilled in managing wealth grasp its proper way and thereby attain abundance naturally. Attending to agriculture and restraining expenditure are the way to produce wealth. If this way can indeed be put into practice, how could the state lack sufficient resources? Now, that by which people are gathered together is called wealth: a state without wealth cannot truly be a state. That by which wealth is managed is called righteousness: wealth without righteousness cannot truly be wealth. Thus the gentleman has a proper way of producing wealth; he certainly need not…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
損下以益上而經制得宜自有以裕於國也其
爲道也又甚大焉固不必損上以益下而公私
兩利亦有以裕於民也然則何如蓋天地本有
自然之利而國家本有惟正之供惟其力之不
勤而用之無節故恒見其不足耳誠能驅天下
之民而歸諸農其生之也既無遺利矣又且汰
冗員裁冗費不使有浮食焉盡三時之勤以服
乎耕其爲之也既無遺力矣又且量所入爲所
出不使有侈用焉斯則勤以務本而財之入也
===
無窮儉以制用而財之出也有限以無窮之財
供有限之用是以下常給而上常餘雖國有大
事而内府外府之儲自將取之而不匱矣百姓
足而君亦足雖年或大侵而三年九年之蓄自
可恃之以無恐矣謂之大道信乎其爲謀國經
久之計而非一切權宜之術可比也然則有國
家者豈必外本内末而後財可聚哉嘗觀周禮
一書其論理財詳矣大約不外此四者至所謂
九式節財用者尤惓惓焉蓋天地生財止有此

爲道也又甚大焉爾不必損上以益下而公私

自然之利而國家本有惟正之供惟其力之不
勤而用之無節故恒見其不足耳誠能驅天下
之民而歸諸農其生之也既無遺利矣又且法
冗員裁冗費不使有浮食焉盡三時之勤以服
乎耕其爲之也既無遺力矣又且量所入爲所
出不使有侈用焉斯則勤以務本而財之入也

punctuated: 損下以益上，而經制得宜，自有以裕於國也。其爲道也，又甚大焉。固不必損上以益下，而公私兩利，亦有以裕於民也。然則何如？蓋天地本有自然之利，而國家本有惟正之供。惟其力之不勤，而用之無節，故恒見其不足耳。誠能驅天下之民而歸諸農，其生之也既無遺利矣；又且汰冗員，裁冗費，不使有浮食焉。盡三時之勤以服乎耕，其爲之也既無遺力矣；又且量所入爲所出，不使有侈用焉。斯則勤以務本，而財之入也無窮；儉以制用，而財之出也有限。以無窮之財，供有限之用，是以下常給而上常餘。雖國有大事，而内府外府之儲，自將取之而不匱矣。百姓足而君亦足，雖年或大侵，而三年九年之蓄，自可恃之以無恐矣。謂之大道，信乎其爲謀國經久之計，而非一切權宜之術可比也。然則有國家者，豈必外本内末而後財可聚哉？嘗觀《周禮》一書，其論理財詳矣。大約不外此四者，至所謂九式節財用者，尤惓惓焉。蓋天地生財止有此
translation_en:
…diminish the resources of those below to benefit those above: with financial institutions properly ordered, there are naturally means to enrich the state. This way of proceeding has still broader implications. There is certainly no need to diminish the resources of those above to benefit those below; when public and private interests both benefit, there are also means to enrich the people. How, then, is this to be done? Heaven and earth inherently yield natural benefits, and the state has its regular, legitimate revenues. It is only because labor is insufficiently diligent and expenditure unrestrained that resources constantly appear inadequate. If the people throughout the realm can indeed be directed back to agriculture, their production will leave no source of profit untapped. Furthermore, redundant personnel should be dismissed and unnecessary expenses curtailed, so that none consume without contributing. If they devote the full labor of the three farming seasons to cultivation, no effort will be spared in their work. Furthermore, expenditure should be measured against income, allowing no extravagant consumption.

Thus, through diligent attention to the fundamental occupation of agriculture, the inflow of wealth will be inexhaustible; through frugal regulation of expenditure, its outflow will be limited. With inexhaustible resources meeting limited expenses, those below will always have enough, and those above will always have a surplus. Even when the state faces major undertakings, the reserves of the inner and outer treasuries will naturally be available without being exhausted. When the common people have enough, their ruler will also have enough. Even if a year brings severe famine, reserves sufficient for three or nine years can be relied upon without fear. To call this the great way is surely justified: it is a lasting plan for governing the state, incomparable with any merely expedient technique. Must those who rule a state, then, slight the fundamental occupation and favor secondary pursuits before wealth can be accumulated?

I have examined the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), which discusses financial administration in detail. Broadly speaking, it does not go beyond these four measures. It is especially insistent on what it calls regulating financial expenditure through the nine standards. For the wealth produced by heaven and earth amounts only to this…

數。舍力本節用而求足國之策，則桑孔之徒專取民財者耳，君子所不道也。《書》曰：「慎乃儉德，惟懷永圖。」司國計者尚其念之。
子曰：「先進於禮樂，野人也；後進於禮樂，君子也。如用之，則吾從先進。」

聖人於禮樂，述時人之所尚，表在已之所從，盖文敝則宜捄之以質也。聖人論禮樂而獨從先進也，有以哉！想其意，盖謂禮樂貴在得中，而君子務於實勝。今也或失之靡矣，吾方憂其敝而莫之捄也，而世之論者乃曰：「先進於禮樂，野人也。」盖見其簡而遂以為陋也，見其直而遂以為俚也。是以今而論昔也，則其謂之野人也固宜。「後進於禮樂，君子也。」盖習其繁而以為有度也。
translation_en:
…amount. To abandon diligence in fundamental production and economy in expenditure while seeking a way to enrich the state is merely to follow the likes of Sang and Kong, who concentrated on taking wealth from the people. This is something a gentleman will not advocate. The Book of Documents says: “Be heedful of your virtue of frugality; cherish plans for the long term.” May those responsible for the state's finances bear this in mind.
The Master said: “The earlier generations, in their practice of rites and music, were country people; the later generations, in their practice of rites and music, are gentlemen. If I were to employ these practices, I would follow the earlier generations.”
Shi Ke
Associate Examiner Lü, Bureau Director, comments: “Restrained and unadorned, elegant and well ordered: this is a work that returns to antiquity. Accept it.”
Associate Examiner Shen, Left Mentor, comments: “Clear, fluent, classically elegant: it sweeps away all vulgarity and may serve as a model.”
Examiner Lü, Academician, comments: “Its writing and meaning are substantial and rounded; the author aspires to return to antiquity.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “A work of antique elegance.”
In discussing rites and music, the sage described what his contemporaries esteemed and declared what he himself would follow, for when refinement becomes corrupt, it should be remedied with substance. Surely the sage had a reason for following only the earlier generations when discussing rites and music! We may suppose his meaning to have been this: what matters in rites and music is attaining the proper mean, while the gentleman strives to give substance precedence. Nowadays, they may have erred toward extravagance. I am troubled by their corruption, which no one remedies, yet contemporary commentators say: “The earlier generations, in their practice of rites and music, were country people.” Seeing their simplicity, they therefore regard them as crude; seeing their directness, they therefore regard them as rustic. This is judging the past by the present, so it is only to be expected that they should call them country people. “The later generations, in their practice of rites and music, are gentlemen.” This is because, accustomed to their complexity, they regard them as possessing proper measure…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
習其縟而以爲有章也是以今而論今也則其
謂之君子也亦宜夫習俗易以移人而古道乖
其所好世固如此若我用之則願從先進何
也禮樂所以養德也而養德者宜處其實不宜
處其華所以維風也而維風者宜居其厚不宜
居其薄以求諸實先進有焉有其實則用以治
心而心平用以治身而身正周公之懿範猶存
固吾所夢想者也雖戾於俗奚恤乎以求諸厚
先進有焉有其厚則用之朝廷而化行用之邦
===
國而俗美文武之遺風未泯固吾所憲章者也
雖以爲野何傷乎吁夫子此言其欲挽衰世以
復乎成周之盛意獨至矣然文勝之弊卒與周
相爲終始而莫之能捄豈世之喜文而惡質也
猶江河之日趨於下而不可復返耶抑轉移化
導之機在上而不在下雖以孔子之聖而無位
亦不能使民之信且從耶有世道之任者當知
所從事矣
有安社稷臣者以安社稷爲悅者也有天

雖以爲野何傷乎吁夫子此言其欲挽衰救以
復乎成周之盛意獨至矣然文勝之弊卒與周
相爲終始而莫之能捄豈世之喜文而惡質也
猶江河之日趨於下而不可復返耶抑轉移化

亦不能使民之信且從耶有世道之任者嘗知
所從事矣
有安社稷臣者以安社稷爲悅者也有天
punctuated:
習其縟而以爲有章也。是以今而論今也，則其謂之君子也亦宜。夫習俗易以移人，而古道乖其所好，世固如此。若我用之，則願從先進。何也？禮樂所以養德也，而養德者宜處其實，不宜處其華；所以維風也，而維風者宜居其厚，不宜居其薄。以求諸實，先進有焉。有其實，則用以治心而心平，用以治身而身正。周公之懿範猶存，固吾所夢想者也，雖戾於俗奚恤乎？以求諸厚，先進有焉。有其厚，則用之朝廷而化行，用之邦國而俗美。文武之遺風未泯，固吾所憲章者也，雖以爲野何傷乎？吁！夫子此言，其欲挽衰世以復乎成周之盛，意獨至矣。然文勝之弊，卒與周相爲終始，而莫之能捄。豈世之喜文而惡質也，猶江河之日趨於下而不可復返耶？抑轉移化導之機在上而不在下，雖以孔子之聖而無位，亦不能使民之信且從耶？有世道之任者，當知所從事矣。
有安社稷臣者，以安社稷爲悅者也。有天
translation_en:
…They have grown accustomed to its elaborate ornamentation and regard it as orderly refinement. This is judging the present by the standards of the present, so it is also understandable that they call these men gentlemen. Prevailing customs readily change people, while the ancient Way runs counter to their tastes: such indeed is the world. If I were to employ ritual and music, however, I would choose to follow the earlier practitioners. Why? Ritual and music nurture virtue, and those who nurture virtue should abide in substance, not outward splendor. They sustain moral customs, and those who sustain moral customs should dwell in depth, not shallowness. If one seeks substance, the earlier practitioners possess it. With that substance, one can employ ritual and music to govern the heart, and the heart becomes tranquil; to govern oneself, and one becomes upright. The admirable example of the Duke of Zhou still survives: it is precisely what I dream of. Though it runs counter to prevailing customs, why should I worry? If one seeks depth, the earlier practitioners possess it. With that depth, one can employ ritual and music at court, and moral transformation spreads; employ them throughout the realm, and customs become good. The inherited influence of Kings Wen and Wu has not disappeared: it is precisely what I take as my model. Though others deem it rustic, what harm is there in that?
Ah! In these words, the Master’s desire to rescue an age of decline and restore the flourishing order of Zhou reaches its utmost intensity. Yet the harmful predominance of outward refinement ultimately persisted throughout the life of the Zhou, and no one could remedy it. Could it be that the world’s love of refinement and dislike of substance are like rivers flowing ever downward, unable to turn back? Or is it that the power to change and morally guide people rests with those above, not those below, so that even someone as sage as Confucius, lacking office, could not make the people trust and follow him? Those responsible for the moral order of the world should know where to direct their efforts.

…people of Heaven, who act only when they see that their Way can be put into practice throughout the realm. There are great men, who rectify themselves and thereby rectify other things.

Xiong Weixue

Associate Examiner Yuan, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “The diction and ideas are lofty … [?].”
Associate Examiner Song, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “The passages discussing character and achievement, together with the diction, are orderly and dignified. Selected to serve as a model.”
Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler, comments: “The main framework is concise and rigorous. The concluding explanation of Mencius’s praise of himself is especially fine.”
Associate Examiner Luo, Senior Compiler, comments: “The composition is fully integrated; the language and reasoning are clear and fluent.”
Examiner Lü, Academician, comments: “Dignified and classically elegant.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “His discussion of character and accomplishment offers ample evidence of his cultivation.”

When the great worthy assesses scholars, the higher their character, the greater their accomplishments. For the achievements they manifest depend upon the men themselves. Can ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain, people of Heaven, and great men all be discussed indiscriminately? Mencius’s meaning is, I think, that where character differs, achievements also differ. Flattering ministers who ingratiate themselves and seek to please are low in moral bearing. Ascending through the ranks, there are ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain, people of Heaven, and great men. All are gentlemen, but their capacities are unequal.

Ministers who secure the altars of soil and grain take greater thought for the state than for themselves. Above, they seek to correct and assist their ruler, so that the altars of soil and grain have a master; below, they seek to shelter and protect the people, so that the altars of soil and grain have support. Only when the state is securely settled do their hearts find peace along with it. Their ambition thus lies in rendering meritorious service, and their efforts are devoted to repaying their lord. They are loyal, but have not yet attained greatness. As for people of Heaven …

…hold themselves to weighty responsibilities indeed and do not lightly put themselves to the test in office. Only when advancement enables them to put their Way into practice above do they exercise their learning to make their ruler like Yao and Shun; only when advancement enables them to put their Way into practice below do they fulfill their ambition to make the people like Yao and Shun. Should my Way remain forever thwarted, I would rather remain thwarted along with it. Such a person’s aspirations tower over his age, and his Way requires wide implementation. He is great, but has not yet attained transforming greatness.

As for the great man, his nature reaches its utmost in preserving the spiritual, and his dealings with every being manifest the marvel of transformation wherever he passes. His sincerity wins his ruler’s trust: he has the beneficial effect of rectifying the ruler’s heart, yet leaves no visible trace. His virtuous instruction reaches the people: he brings about a transforming order, yet claims no mastery over its achievements. Once I have rectified myself, the court and the myriad states rectify themselves in response. Such a person does not depend on exalted rank to secure the state, yet the altars of soil and grain depend on him for their security; he need not resort to dispensing favors to others, yet all under Heaven receive his blessings. This is greatness that has attained transformation. How consummate!

Differences in human stature have implications such as these [?]. This was what Mengzi meant by the responsibility he took upon himself. He certainly disdained being merely an outstanding scholar of a single state. Yi Yin was an early awakened one among Heaven’s people, yet Mengzi said, “Let us set him aside for now.” His meaning can thus be understood. Kongzi possessed the virtue of the dragon while remaining hidden. The civilizing transformation he could effect was constrained in his own time, yet ten thousand generations have benefited from it. He was the most eminent of great men; hence it was he whom Mengzi wished to emulate.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text invokes the human Way to elucidate the meaning of Qian, attending to the practice of the four virtues through vigor. Vigor is the foundation for practicing virtue. The four virtues are present in human beings, yet it is only through the gentleman’s vigor that they are put into practice. From this the meaning of the canonical text can be understood.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text means this: Qian stands first among the hexagrams, and origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy constitute the completeness of virtue. I have already elucidated their meaning through the Way of Heaven; extending this to the human Way, there is also something to be discerned. Why is this? Heaven endows human beings with a single principle, in which the virtues of origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy are all present. Thus they are the chief of goodness and the convergence of excellence, the harmony of righteousness and the supporting trunk of affairs. Continuing goodness and bringing nature to completion—are these not the universally operative virtues throughout the world?

The gentleman fully realizes his nature through this single principle, and thus possesses the virtues of origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy in their entirety. Hence, by embodying benevolence he can lead others, and by bringing excellence together, ritual propriety…

translation_en:
…ritual propriety can be accorded with; by benefiting things, righteousness can be brought into harmony, and through steadfast firmness, affairs can be given their sustaining framework. In fully embodying one’s human form and fulfilling one’s nature, is it only the gentleman who possesses complete capacity? Why is this so? It is truly because the gentleman embodies the firmness of Heaven’s virtue. Through firmness he does not yield to material desires; thus the complete substance of the four virtues remains unencumbered. All six lines of Qian are yang: firmness in its utmost degree. Is this not why origination, success, benefit, and constancy are all comprised within it, with none lying outside? The gentleman models himself on the vigor of Heaven’s movement. Through vigor he is not deflected by selfish intentions; thus the wondrous functioning of the four virtues is inexhaustible. Qian is substantial throughout: vigor in its utmost degree. Can it be without significance that origination, success, benefit, and constancy are all fully present, without partiality? By observing the gentleman, we recognize the subtle meaning of the classic’s text. Does not the Changes comprehend the Way of both Heaven and humanity!
Moreover, King Wen’s appended judgment on Qian and Confucius’s Commentary on the Judgments both embody the essence of the teaching of the mind [?]. Heaven’s Way moves without stagnation; the sage’s mind is pure and unceasing. What made King Wen worthy of the designation “Wen” was his purity. Thus he set forth in Qian the Changes as understood in his own mind [?]. Confucius inherited the succession from King Wen, and therefore expounded in his commentary what he took as his model. Is this not what makes the Way of the Changes great!
“One who possesses greatness must not become full of himself; therefore it is followed by Qian (Modesty). One who possesses greatness and can remain modest will surely experience joy; therefore it is followed by Yu (Joy).”

聖人序卦，有謙之所當崇者，有豫之所由致者。蓋謙也者，帝王之盛節也。以之處有，以之致豫，孰能外哉？且夫天下之治亂者，時也；盛衰者，幾也。而惟時惟幾，勅天之命，以保大定功者，聖人也。觀於卦序見矣。彼地中有山，謙之象也，而以次有者何？夫有而曰大，土之廣也，民之衆也，有易盈之慮焉。是故撫亨大之運者，存挹損之戒者也。願欲畢遂矣，不可生侈而長驕，上焉天命之難諶也；志意既廣矣，不可凌節而踰制，下焉民心之易失也。蓋有不可恃，謙有有而不居之義，則處有之道莫善於謙矣。大有受之以謙者，以此。雷出地奮，豫之象也，而以次謙者何？夫有而能謙，德之盛也，禮之恭也，有受益之道焉。是

Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler, comments: “Dignified and elegant; refined in meaning and composition [?].”
Associate Examiner Luo, Senior Compiler, comments: “Pure, correct, and classically elegant—the work of someone deeply versed in the Book of Changes.”

In arranging the hexagrams, the sage showed why Modesty must be honored and how Contentment may be attained. Modesty is the crowning virtue of emperors and kings. It enables them to conduct themselves amid abundance and to attain contentment. Who could dispense with it? Order and disorder in the world depend upon the times; flourishing and decline depend upon the incipient tendencies of events. It is the sage who attends to these times and tendencies and reverently carries out Heaven’s mandate, thereby preserving greatness and securing achievement. This can be seen in the sequence of the hexagrams.

A mountain within the earth is the image of Modesty. Why, then, does it follow Possession? When possession is called “great,” it means broad territory and a numerous population; there is reason to fear that complacency may easily arise. Thus, one who presides over an age of great prosperity keeps in mind the admonition to restrain and diminish oneself. Though all wishes and desires have been fulfilled, one must not become extravagant or foster arrogance: above, Heaven’s mandate is difficult to rely upon. Though aspirations have expanded, one must not overstep proper bounds or exceed established limits: below, the people’s allegiance is easily lost. Possessions cannot be relied upon. Modesty signifies possessing without claiming credit; hence, no way of conducting oneself amid abundance is better than modesty. This is why Great Possession is followed by Modesty.

translation_en:
… Thus those who foster a spirit of humility and deference enjoy the blessings of peace and harmony. When good government has already been achieved, yet one acts as though it had not, boundless solicitude will also bring boundless blessings. When the state is already secure, yet one acts as though it were not, those who worry before all under Heaven will take their pleasure after all under Heaven. Humility assuredly has a good outcome, and Yu (Contentment) conveys the harmony and joy of people’s hearts; thus the blessings of a good outcome find their confirmation in Yu. This is why Qian (Humility) is followed by Yu. How subtle is the meaning of the Sequence of the Hexagrams! I have reflected on the government of Yao and Shun: lofty and vast, it defies description. Yet the ruler and his ministers then admonished and encouraged one another, working diligently without cease. Not only did they take no credit for what they possessed; they were not even conscious of possessing it. Their transforming influence brought concord and spread like the wind, beyond anything later ages could attain. Thus Yao and Shun’s achievement of good government merely by letting their robes hang down drew upon Qian (Heaven) and Kun (Earth), while their preservation of good government through vigilance and diligence drew upon Qian (Humility). Those who study the Changes understand this.
Book of Documents
Gao Yao said: “Ah! It lies in knowing people and bringing peace to the people.” Yu said: “Ah! To accomplish all this—even the emperor finds it difficult. Knowing people is wisdom: it enables one to appoint people to office. Bringing peace to the people is benevolence: the common people cherish such a ruler.”
Huang Hongxian

大臣以智仁責難于君，而同列發其義焉。夫知人安民，智仁之德備矣。以此兼盡，豈非克艱之道哉？且夫致治必先于迪德，而君德莫大于智仁。臯陶陳謨而未盡其旨，乃嘆美言曰：「為政在人，甄别而進退之者君也。必度德量才，俾權度弗爽，而賢雋皆得以奮庸焉，斯智之德允迪矣。保邦在民，奠麗而輯寧之者君也。必敷政施教，俾膏澤無壅，而生民咸得以立命焉，斯仁之德允迪矣。」是道也，語其至，則聖有所不能；兼其難，則堯猶以為病。正帝之所當克艱者也。禹乃致嘆以發之曰：「知人安民，道至大也。既仁且智，帝其難之，何也？賢才至衆，知有所遺，非智也。曰知人，則明哲無疆，而建官位事罔弗宜矣，豈易能耶？民生至廣，愛有未徧，非仁也。曰安民，則惠德有孚，而近悅遠來罔不懷矣，豈易盡耶？」盖知人

Examiner Lü, a Hanlin Academician, comments: 〔Classically elegant and grounded in practical realities.〕

A great minister charges his ruler with the difficult duties of wisdom and benevolence, and a fellow minister expounds their meaning. In knowing men and bringing peace to the people, the virtues of wisdom and benevolence are complete. To fulfill both together—is this not the way to master difficulty? Indeed, achieving good government must begin with practicing virtue, and among a ruler’s virtues none is greater than wisdom and benevolence. Gao Yao had offered his counsel but had not yet exhausted its meaning. He therefore exclaimed in admiration: “Government depends on men; it is the ruler who distinguishes among them and advances or dismisses them. He must assess their virtue and weigh their abilities, ensuring that his standards do not err and that all worthy and talented men can exert themselves in service. Only then is the virtue of wisdom truly practiced. Preserving the state depends on the people; it is the ruler who settles them securely and brings them harmony and peace. He must carry out policies and extend instruction, ensuring that his beneficence flows unobstructed and that all the people can secure their livelihoods. Only then is the virtue of benevolence truly practiced.” To speak of this Way in its utmost perfection, even a sage has things he cannot accomplish; to undertake its difficulties together, even Yao regarded this as arduous. These are precisely the difficulties that the emperor ought to master.
Yu then sighed and expounded the point, saying: “Knowing men and bringing peace to the people constitute a supremely great Way. To be both benevolent and wise—even the emperor finds this difficult. Why? Worthy and talented men are exceedingly numerous; if one’s discernment overlooks any, that is not wisdom. To speak of knowing men means possessing boundless discernment, so that in establishing offices and assigning duties nothing is inappropriate. How could this be easy to accomplish? The people are exceedingly many; if one’s care does not reach them all, that is not benevolence. To speak of bringing peace to the people means that one’s beneficent virtue inspires trust, so that those nearby rejoice and those far away come, and none fails to cherish the ruler. translation_en:
…provides the foundation for bringing peace to the people, while bringing peace to the people realizes the achievement of discerning worthy men. Either undertaking is difficult enough; accomplishing both is especially difficult. Hence the saying: “Even the emperor finds this difficult.” How profound was the intention of Yu and Gao Yao in urging these demanding duties upon one another! Considering the age of Tang and Yu, no worthy man remained overlooked in the countryside, and all the states were at peace. In discerning worthy men and bringing peace to the people, Yao and Shun should therefore have had nothing wanting. Yet Gao Yao demanded this of Shun, and Yu spoke of its difficulty even for Yao. Why? Because the sage’s aspiration for good government is inexhaustible, as is the great minister’s devotion to his ruler. Thus the practice of mutual admonition in the age of Tang and Yu established the supreme standard for rulers and ministers for all ages.

“From morning until the sun had passed its zenith, he had no leisure to eat, thereby bringing harmony to all the people.”
By Fang Yang.

The sage king’s diligence in government consists simply in keeping his heart fixed upon all under Heaven. For the ultimate aim of the kingly way is that all the people should find their proper place. With King Wen so deeply concerned for the people, how could he have leisure to indulge in ease?

text:
且夫君身之勞逸萬姓之安危係焉居已于逸
而能置天下于安者否也無逸者其惟文王乎
蓋其擴柔恭之德既發政以施仁存抑畏之心
尤勵精以圖治自朝至于日中自中至于日昃
以其時則甚久矣昧爽而視朝日昃而忘食以
其身則甚勞矣而文王之心蓋曰萬民至衆匹
夫匹婦有不被澤者乎吾憂也憂之深故圖之
不容以不亟安民至難仁心仁政有未及民者
乎吾責也責之重故爲之不敢以不勤推吾惠
===
鮮之仁不獨使西土怙冒而已將躋一世于太
和而雍熙之俗成焉此其心有不能一日安者
雖欲暇食也得乎充吾懷保之念不獨使汝墳
遵化而已將囿萬邦于恊和而樂利之風普焉
此其心有不能一息懈者欲無旰食也得乎夫
勞在于一身澤加于天下文王之無逸大矣而
嗣王可弗監哉抑周家王業由文王勤勞成之
信矣然獄慎又罔敢知何也蓋日不暇給罔非
後世代有司之任者所爲而宅俊是求則政又

punctuated: 且夫君身之勞逸，萬姓之安危係焉。居已于逸，而能置天下于安者，否也。無逸者，其惟文王乎！蓋其擴柔恭之德，既發政以施仁；存抑畏之心，尤勵精以圖治。自朝至于日中，自中至于日昃，以其時則甚久矣；昧爽而視朝，日昃而忘食，以其身則甚勞矣。而文王之心蓋曰：「萬民至衆，匹夫匹婦有不被澤者乎？吾憂也。」憂之深，故圖之不容以不亟。「安民至難，仁心仁政有未及民者乎？吾責也。」責之重，故爲之不敢以不勤。推吾惠鮮之仁，不獨使西土怙冒而已，將躋一世于太和，而雍熙之俗成焉。此其心有不能一日安者，雖欲暇食也，得乎？充吾懷保之念，不獨使汝墳遵化而已，將囿萬邦于恊和，而樂利之風普焉。此其心有不能一息懈者，欲無旰食也，得乎？夫勞在于一身，澤加于天下，文王之無逸大矣，而嗣王可弗監哉！抑周家王業由文王勤勞成之，信矣。然獄慎又罔敢知，何也？蓋日不暇給，罔非後世代有司之任者所爲，而宅俊是求，則政又
translation_en:
Moreover, the security or peril of the myriad people depends upon whether their ruler labors or takes his ease. Could someone settle himself in ease yet bring security to all under Heaven? No. Was it not King Wen above all who shunned ease? He extended his gentle and reverent virtue, issuing measures to bestow benevolence; he preserved a humble and apprehensive heart, applying himself still more earnestly to achieving good government. From morning until noon, and from noon until the sun declined: in duration, this was very long indeed. Holding court at daybreak and forgetting to eat when the sun declined: for his person, this was very arduous indeed. Yet King Wen’s heart must have said: “The people are so numerous. Is there any ordinary man or woman who has not received my beneficence? This is my concern.” Because his concern was profound, he could not but urgently devise means to address it. “Bringing peace to the people is exceedingly difficult. Is there any benevolent intention or policy that has yet to reach them? This is my responsibility.” Because his responsibility was weighty, he dared not pursue it without diligence.

Extending his benevolence in cherishing those in need, he sought not merely to give the western lands protection and shelter, but to raise an entire age to supreme harmony, establishing customs of concord and prosperity. Thus his heart could not rest easy for even a day. Even if he wished for leisure to eat, could he have it? Giving full scope to his resolve to cherish and protect, he sought not merely to bring the people along the banks of the Ru River under his transforming influence, but to embrace the myriad states in concord, spreading everywhere a spirit of contentment and well-being. Thus his heart could not slacken for even a moment. Could he avoid delaying his meals until late in the day?

The labor fell upon one person, while its benefits reached all under Heaven. Great indeed was King Wen’s refusal of ease! Could succeeding kings fail to take him as their example? Now, it is certainly true that the royal enterprise of the house of Zhou was accomplished through King Wen’s diligent toil. Yet why did he not presume to take personal charge of lawsuits and matters requiring caution? Being so occupied that the day affords insufficient time is precisely what results when rulers of later ages take over the responsibilities of the officials in charge. But in seeking out and appointing men of outstanding ability, in governing he also …

Associate Examiner Shen, Examining Editor, comments: “Being careful and luminously serving is exceedingly difficult to grasp; this composition captures it.”

That the sage serves Heaven with reverence manifests the fullness of his virtue. Virtue gathers in reverence. Serving Heaven with a careful and reverent heart, how abundant was King Wen’s virtue! The Greater Ode Great Brightness celebrates ancestral virtue. Here it traces the reason King Wen received the Mandate, saying: “Heaven favors a ruler for his virtue; a ruler serves Heaven through his heart. When I consider King Wen’s heart, I see that he did not regard his being first to reach the shore of the Way as grounds for pride and self-aggrandizement. The more expansive his heart became, the more he gathered it inward…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
而儼乎上帝之監觀不以聖域之優入焉可縱
焉以自放也愈收斂則愈精明而凛乎上帝之
陟降知識弗用翼翼然若有所制而是心之默
順皆天也與下濟之光相對越焉緝熈閤間翼
翼然若有所勉而是心之敬止皆天也與於昭
之神相左右焉出往游衍帝之明命無日不臨
也而齋戒於中者亦無一息之少懈盖即此神
明之德以仰答於上而文之事天也昭昭矣奚
待殷薦而後為事耶動靜起居帝之明威隨在
===
皆察也而退藏於中者亦無一事之少違盖即
此洗心之密以祗事乎天而天之昭格也有素
矣豈必將享而始為事耶吁文德之盛端在於
此懐多福而膺眷命有以也夫書曰皇天無親
克敬惟親世之逸豫之主每以天不足畏敬不
足行此安危理亂之所由分而周公之所為惓
惓於成王也厥後成王以其不敢康之心夙夜
基命無亦因公之言而有得於小心之家法乎
自彼氐羌莫敢不來享莫敢不來王曰商

皆察也而退藏於中者亦無一事之少違蓋即

克敬惟親世之逸豫之主每以天不足畏敬不
足行此安危理亂之所由分而周公之所爲惓
惓於成王也厥後成王以其不敢康之心夙夜
基命無亦因公之言而有得於小心之家法乎
自彼氐羌莫敢不來享莫敢不來王曰商
punctuated:
而儼乎上帝之監觀。不以聖域之優入焉可縱焉以自放也，愈收斂則愈精明，而凛乎上帝之陟降。知識弗用，翼翼然若有所制，而是心之默順皆天也，與下濟之光相對越焉；緝熈閤間，翼翼然若有所勉，而是心之敬止皆天也，與於昭之神相左右焉。出往游衍，帝之明命無日不臨也，而齋戒於中者亦無一息之少懈。盖即此神明之德以仰答於上，而文之事天也昭昭矣，奚待殷薦而後為事耶？動靜起居，帝之明威隨在皆察也，而退藏於中者亦無一事之少違。盖即此洗心之密以祗事乎天，而天之昭格也有素矣，豈必將享而始為事耶？吁！文德之盛，端在於此。懐多福而膺眷命，有以也夫！《書》曰：「皇天無親，克敬惟親。」世之逸豫之主，每以天不足畏，敬不足行，此安危理亂之所由分，而周公之所為惓惓於成王也。厥後成王以其不敢康之心，夙夜基命，無亦因公之言而有得於小心之家法乎？

自彼氐羌，莫敢不來享，莫敢不來王，曰商
translation_en:
…and stood in awe of the Lord on High’s watchful gaze. He did not regard his effortless entry into the realm of sagehood as license to indulge himself and cast off restraint. The more he restrained himself, the more discerning he became, standing in awe of the Lord on High’s ascending and descending presence. He employed no intellectual contrivance; reverently cautious, as though held in check, his heart’s silent submission accorded wholly with Heaven, answering the light that reaches down from above. Continuing in brightness within the inner chamber [?], reverently cautious, as though urged onward, his heart’s abiding reverence accorded wholly with Heaven, accompanied on either side by the brightly manifest spirit. Wherever he went or wandered, not a day passed without the Lord’s luminous command looking down upon him; nor did his inward purification and vigilance slacken for even a single breath. Through this very virtue of spiritual illumination, he responded to the power above: King Wen’s service to Heaven was thus plainly manifest. Why should he have waited for grand sacrificial offerings before serving it? Whether moving or still, rising or resting, he was everywhere observed by the Lord’s manifest majesty; and in the hidden recesses of his heart, he departed from it in not a single matter. Through this very meticulous cleansing of his heart, he reverently served Heaven; Heaven’s manifest presence had therefore long been with him. Surely he did not begin serving it only when about to make an offering?

Ah! The fullness of King Wen’s virtue lay precisely here. There was good reason why he received abundant blessings and Heaven’s gracious mandate! The Book of Documents says: “August Heaven has no partial affections; it favors only those capable of reverence.” Indolent rulers commonly suppose that Heaven need not be feared and reverence need not be practiced. Here lies the division between security and peril, order and disorder; this is why the Duke of Zhou addressed King Cheng with such earnest concern. Thereafter, King Cheng, with a heart that dared not seek ease, labored morning and night to establish the mandate. Was it not through the Duke’s words that he gained an understanding of his house’s inherited practice of vigilant care?

“From those Di and Qiang, none dared fail to come presenting offerings; none dared fail to come acknowledging the king. It was Shang…”

The worthy king recounts the sincerity with which distant foreign peoples served Shang, making clear the grounds for reproaching Chu. Even the Di and Qiang, distant as they were, served Shang sincerely and dared not disobey; how much more should Jingchu have done so? It was fitting that Gaozong should proclaim this great principle and thereby reproach them.
The king spoke thus: “You people of Jingchu rely on your remoteness and fail to attend court. Have you also heard of the age of Cheng Tang? His receiving offerings and jade, and serving as a model throughout the nine regions, cannot be comprehensively recounted [?]; those in the guest and remote service zones surrounding the four outer borders are too numerous to enumerate. Let us speak just of the Di and Qiang: none were more distant than these. Though they produced no rare treasures, they nevertheless came with the other states to present offerings. At the proper seasons they offered their local products, as though someone had summoned them; none dared neglect this duty. Though they were not among those who wore ceremonial caps and girdles, they nevertheless came with the other states to acknowledge the king. Generation after generation they came to behold his brilliant glory, as though someone had appointed a time for them; none dared arrive late. Yet their coming…

所屬則中國有常尊自正域以來其制已一定
而未之有改矣天府所藏則外夷有常憲自方
命以後其道已四達而莫之或悖矣是商固未

豈廹於不得已而出於不可繼者耶蓋曰居薄
之世莫非其土我氐羌亦商土也以供土貢則
禮然而敢不享歟食商之土莫非其臣我氐羌
亦商臣也以述臣職則禮然而敢不王歟天命
所屬則中國有常尊自正域以來其制已一定
而本之有攸矣天府所藏則外夷有常憲自方
命以後其遺已四達而莫之或悖矣是商固未
始越其常而過求於我而我又何敢失其常而
自外於商哉氐羌之在昔也如彼荆楚之在今
===
也如此湯嘗之奮伐亦執商之常以問夫不享
不王之罪爾夫豈黷武者哉抑論高宗丕纘湯
緒肇域四海然當時幅幀南盡乎荆楚西不過
氐羌蓋舌之不勤遠畧如此楚在江漢間不得
已而用其猶自以為罙入而亟於文告至稱引
氐羌以勤之噫其犯順則威撻之如荆楚其慕
義則禮接之如氐羌豈惟有商固萬世帝王禦
夷之常道也
春秋
punctuated:
豈迫於不得已而出於不可繼者耶？蓋曰：「居商之世，莫非其土，我氐羌亦商土也。以供土實，則禮然，而敢不享歟？食商之土，莫非其臣，我氐羌亦商臣也。以遂臣職，則禮然，而敢不王歟？天命所屬，則中國有常尊，自正域以來，其制已一定而未之有改矣。天府所藏，則外夷有常憲，自方命以後，其道已四達而莫之或悖矣。是商固未始越其常而過求於我，而我又何𢠢失其常而自外於商？」吁！氐羌之在昔也如彼，荆楚之在今也如此，湯孫之奮伐，亦執商之常以問夫不享不王之罪耳，夫豈黷武者哉？抑論高宗丕纘湯緒，肇域四海，然當時幅幀南盡乎荆楚，西不過氐羌。蓋古之不勤遠畧如此。楚在江漢間，不得已而用兵，猶自以為深入而亟於文告，至稱引氐羌以動之。意其犯順則威撻之如荆楚，其慕義則禮接之如氐羌。豈惟有商？固萬世帝王禦夷之常道也。

春秋
translation_en:
…could their coming have been compelled by circumstances that left them no choice, and prompted by something that could not be sustained? Rather, they said: “Living in the age of Shang, we find no land that is not its territory; the lands of us Di and Qiang are also Shang territory. To supply the produce of our lands is what ritual propriety requires: how could we dare not present offerings? All who live off Shang’s land are its subjects; we Di and Qiang are also Shang subjects. To discharge a subject’s duties is what ritual propriety requires: how could we dare not attend the royal court? Since the Mandate of Heaven rests with Shang, the central realm holds enduring supremacy. Ever since the territories were set in order, this arrangement has been firmly established and never altered. The statutes preserved in Heaven’s treasury provide enduring rules for the peoples beyond the realm. Ever since commands were issued to the regions, this Way has extended in all directions, and none has contravened it. Shang has never departed from its constant norms to make excessive demands upon us; why, then, should we [?] abandon those norms and exclude ourselves from Shang?”

Ah! Such was the conduct of the Di and Qiang in former times, while such is the conduct of Jingchu today! When Tang’s descendant launches a punitive expedition, he merely upholds Shang’s constant norms to call them to account for failing to present offerings and attend the royal court. How could this be wanton warfare?

Now consider Gaozong: he grandly continued Tang’s legacy and established his dominion within the Four Seas. Yet the territorial extent [?] of his time reached only as far south as Jingchu and no farther west than the Di and Qiang. Such was the restraint of the ancients in undertaking distant conquests. Chu lay between the Jiang and Han rivers. Even when compelled to employ troops there, he still considered himself to have penetrated deeply and urgently issued proclamations, going so far as to invoke the Di and Qiang to move them. His intent was that those who defied rightful authority should be chastised with force, as Jingchu was, while those drawn to righteousness should be received with ritual courtesy, as the Di and Qiang were. Was this true only of Shang? It is indeed the constant Way by which emperors and kings in every age govern relations with peoples beyond the realm.

Spring and Autumn Annals

translation_en:
In autumn, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and representatives of Jiang and Huang met at Yanggu. [Third year of Duke Xi.] In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the duke joined the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao in invading Cai. Cai collapsed. They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to the army to conclude a covenant; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling. [Both entries are from the fourth year of Duke Xi.]
In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Xiaozhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the jihai day, they jointly concluded a covenant at Xi. [Ninth year of Duke Xiang.] The duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Xiaozhu in attacking Zheng. They met at Xiaoyu. [Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.]
Wu Xiu

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
則可攻可守而敵國不敢抗吾得齊桓焉當夫
貫澤之盟講而楚勢日孤自輕敵者言之孰不
曰多助在我翦此後食乎桓則謂方漢之險未
易以長驅也廼陽穀徵會定伐楚之謀焉於八
國則命之合而攻於江黃則命之分而守以正
合以奇分盖不待疆埸奏凱而敵已在目中矣
未幾陘亭次而召陵盟江漢以北自是免左衽
之憂則陽穀之始謀耳傳曰先為不可勝以待
敵之可勝其桓公之謂乎又聞兵有二幾勞逸
===
是也識其幾而善處之則知彼知己而敵國不
能乘吾得晉悼焉當夫鄵門之衆集而楚救將
至自好勝者言之孰不曰成師以出固敵是求
乎悼則謂乘廣之雄未易以力角也廼于戲振
旅定駕楚之謀焉在彼則欲戰而不得在我則
能戰而不貪彼常勞我常逸盖不必原野暴骨
而敵已無長技矣未幾東門師而蕭魚會溱洧
以南自是有息肩之日則于戲之成算耳傳曰
兵戢而時動動則威其悼公之謂乎用是知齊

punctuated: 則可攻可守，而敵國不敢抗，吾得齊桓焉。當夫貫澤之盟講，而楚勢日孤，自輕敵者言之，孰不曰：「多助在我，翦此後食乎？」桓則謂方漢之險，未易以長驅也。廼陽穀徵會，定伐楚之謀焉。於八國則命之合而攻，於江黃則命之分而守，以正合，以奇分，盖不待疆埸奏凱，而敵已在目中矣。未幾，陘亭次而召陵盟，江漢以北，自是免左衽之憂，則陽穀之始謀耳。傳曰：「先為不可勝，以待敵之可勝。」其桓公之謂乎？又聞兵有二幾，勞逸是也。識其幾而善處之，則知彼知己，而敵國不能乘，吾得晉悼焉。當夫鄵門之衆集，而楚救將至，自好勝者言之，孰不曰：「成師以出，固敵是求乎？」悼則謂乘廣之雄，未易以力角也。廼于戲振旅，定駕楚之謀焉。在彼則欲戰而不得，在我則能戰而不貪，彼常勞，我常逸，盖不必原野暴骨，而敵已無長技矣。未幾，東門師而蕭魚會，溱洧以南，自是有息肩之日，則于戲之成算耳。傳曰：「兵戢而時動，動則威。」其悼公之謂乎？用是知齊
translation_en:
…then one can attack or defend, and enemy states dare not resist. I find this exemplified in Duke Huan of Qi. When the covenant at Guanze had been concluded and Chu’s position grew more isolated by the day, who among those who underestimated the enemy would not have said, “We have abundant support: should we not destroy this enemy before taking our meal?” Huan, however, judged that the natural defenses of Fang and the Han River could not readily be overcome by a deep advance. He therefore summoned an assembly at Yanggu and settled the plan for attacking Chu. He ordered the eight states to combine their forces and attack, while ordering Jiang and Huang to deploy separately and defend. He combined forces for orthodox operations and divided them for unorthodox operations. Thus, even before victory was proclaimed on the frontier, the enemy was already within his grasp. Soon afterward, his forces encamped at Xingting and concluded a covenant at Shaoling. From then on, the lands north of the Jiang and Han rivers were spared the danger of wearing their robes fastened on the left—that is, of coming under barbarian rule. This resulted from the plan first laid at Yanggu. A transmitted text says, “First make yourself invincible, then await the enemy’s vulnerability.” Does this not describe Duke Huan?

I have also heard that warfare has two critical conditions: exhaustion and ease. If one recognizes these conditions and handles them well, one knows both the enemy and oneself, and enemy states cannot exploit an opening. I find this exemplified in Duke Dao of Jin. When the host had assembled at the gate of Cao and Chu’s relief forces were about to arrive, who among those eager for victory would not have said, “We have marched out with an army fully formed: surely it is the enemy we seek?” Dao, however, judged that the might of Chu’s chariot formations could not readily be matched by force. He therefore withdrew his troops at Yuxi and settled the plan for wearing Chu down through repeated campaigns. The enemy wished to fight but could not; our forces could fight but were not eager to do so. The enemy was continually exhausted, while we remained continually at ease. Thus, without having to expose soldiers’ bones on the open plains, the enemy was already deprived of any effective advantage. Soon afterward came the military action at the eastern gate and the meeting at Xiaoyu. From then on, the lands south of the Zhen and Wei rivers enjoyed respite from their burdens. This resulted from the settled strategy at Yuxi. A transmitted text says, “Arms are kept in reserve and employed at the proper time; when employed, they inspire awe.” Does this not describe Duke Dao? From this we know that Qi…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
桓之一匡晉悼之三駕皆好謀成之管仲智罃
教之也然非三國五鄙之政施舎輸積之仁使
民志内輯而財力素完則雖有謀無所用之夫
管仲之才不可及已而絳也亦罃之流亞哉故
曰安危在出令存亡在所任信哉言也
冬十月壬午公子遂會晉趙盾盟于衡雍

translation_en:
…Duke Huan’s unification and rectification of the realm and Duke Dao of Jin’s three campaigns were all accomplished through a love of careful planning, under the guidance of Guan Zhong and Zhi Ying. Yet without the administrative arrangements of the three divisions of the capital and the five outlying districts, and the benevolent measures of granting relief and distributing accumulated supplies, which brought the people’s aspirations into harmony at home and ensured ample financial and material resources beforehand, even the best plans would have had no means of implementation. Guan Zhong’s ability was beyond compare, but was Jiang [Wei Jiang] not also a worthy peer of Ying? Thus it is said: “Security or peril depends on the commands issued; survival or destruction depends on those entrusted with office.” How true these words are!
“In winter, in the tenth month, on renwu, Prince Sui met Zhao Dun of Jin and made a covenant at Hengyong. On yiyou, Prince Sui met the Luo Rong and made a covenant at Bao.” Both entries are from the eighth year of Duke Wen.
Liu Tai
