The Spring and Autumn Annals carefully observes the distinction between the Hua and the Yi, providing particular detail as events require. This shows that the Yi must not be allowed to confound the Hua. In recording the establishment of mutual trust through covenants, the Spring and Autumn Annals draws a sharp distinction between them; its intent is stringent indeed. At the covenants of Hengyong and Bao, the person attending was in both cases Zhong Sui. The ceremonies were completed within a ten-day cycle, and the places were close neighbors: these circumstances alone would not warrant the trouble of recording both in full. 也夷狄外也此天下大防不可一日亂也惟兹
雒邑豈戎之所得居者耶三河錯壤則天地之
奧區焉九鼎卜遷則帝王之都會焉百姓之奸
苗民之裔猶率其衆而居之揆之禹甸是嵩丘
太室可以宅要荒矣考之周疆是卉服穹居可
以稱藩翰矣夫類族以别生重關以禦暴天子
之有道也則曰守在四夷而今周轍不西戎馬
復東奈之何天下無事也於戯伊川之野祭辛
有所𠯁興憂也而此非其明驗乎陸戎之入伐
===
定王所為戒嚴也而此非其厲階乎當時若秦
若晉既延之使入而魯又加親焉將焉用之故
春秋於是二盟再稱公子各日其會正其名與
地以深别之别雒戎於趙盾者正以外戎於雒
也外戎於雒者正以存雒於中國也庶乎族類
明而内外辨經斯世者其懼爾矣抑衡雍之盟
說者謂報于扈也奔命失期而盟以謝過末矣
况以二事出乎盖其時魯文怠緩晉靈幼弱而
不臣如遂者睥睨内外間出入自恣固其所耳

也，夷狄外也。此天下大防，不可一日亂也。惟兹雒邑，豈戎之所得居者耶？三河錯壤，則天地之奧區焉；九鼎卜遷，則帝王之都會焉。百姓之奸，苗民之裔，猶率其衆而居之。揆之禹甸，是嵩丘太室可以宅要荒矣；考之周疆，是卉服穹居可以稱藩翰矣。夫類族以别生，重關以禦暴，天子之有道也。則曰：「守在四夷。」而今周轍不西，戎馬復東，奈之何天下無事也？於戯！伊川之野，祭辛有所𠯁興憂也，而此非其明驗乎？陸戎之入伐，定王所為戒嚴也，而此非其厲階乎？當時若秦若晉，既延之使入，而魯又加親焉，將焉用之？故春秋於是二盟，再稱公子，各日其會，正其名與地，以深别之。别雒戎於趙盾者，正以外戎於雒也；外戎於雒者，正以存雒於中國也。庶乎族類明而内外辨，經斯世者其懼爾矣。
抑衡雍之盟，說者謂報于扈也。奔命失期，而盟以謝過，末矣，况以二事出乎？盖其時魯文怠緩，晉靈幼弱，而不臣如遂者，睥睨内外，間出入自恣，固其所耳。
translation_en:
… lies within, while the Yi and Di lie outside. This is the great boundary of all under Heaven, which must not be confounded for even a single day. Could this city of Luo possibly be a place where the Rong are entitled to dwell? Where the lands of the Three He regions meet, it is the innermost heart of Heaven and Earth; where the relocation of the Nine Tripods was determined by divination, it is the imperial capital. Yet malefactors among the people, descendants of the Miao, still lead their followers to settle there. Judged against the domains ordered by Yu, this would mean that Songqiu and Mount Taishi could accommodate the peoples of the remote outer zones; examined against Zhou’s boundaries, it would mean that those wearing garments of vegetation and living in domed dwellings could be called the realm’s protective bulwarks. To group clans so as to distinguish their peoples, and to establish successive barriers against violence: these are practices of a Son of Heaven who possesses the Way. Hence the saying, “Defence rests with the Yi on the four sides.” But now Zhou’s carriage tracks no longer run westward, while Rong cavalry again move eastward. How could all under Heaven remain free of trouble? Alas! In the countryside of Yichuan, Ji Xin [?] had grounds for apprehension [text unclear]; is this not clear confirmation of it? The invasion by the Lu Rong [?] was what prompted King Ding to order strict defensive precautions; was this not the first step toward that calamity? At the time, Qin and Jin had already invited them to enter, and Lu further cultivated their friendship. What purpose could this serve? Thus, in recording these two covenants, the Spring and Autumn Annals twice uses the designation “ducal son,” dates each meeting separately, and precisely identifies the names and places, thereby drawing a firm distinction. Distinguishing the Rong of Luo from Zhao Dun serves precisely to treat the Rong as outsiders in Luo; treating the Rong as outsiders in Luo serves precisely to preserve Luo as part of the Central States. In this way, perhaps distinctions among peoples may be made clear and the boundary between inside and outside discerned. Those who govern this world should take warning.
Furthermore, commentators say that the covenant at Hengyong was a response to the meeting at Hu. To hurry forth under orders, miss the appointed time, and then make a covenant to apologize for the fault is already a paltry proceeding; how much more so to go out on two such affairs? At that time, Duke Wen of Lu was indolent and dilatory, and Duke Ling of Jin was young and weak. Someone as insubordinate as Sui, casting covetous glances both within and beyond the state, would naturally exploit opportunities to come and go and indulge his own will.

濡既久則檢束於威儀者自固覿其德肅然而

translation_en:
…an impulse that cannot possibly cease—how great is the joy within his heart! Nor does it end there. After prolonged immersion and nurture, his discipline in maintaining a dignified bearing naturally becomes firm. Observe his virtue: solemn and reverent, vigilant and respectful. The disposition of concentrating on the One without distraction is thereby revealed. Once his cultivation has become pure, what manifests itself in his movements and repose is naturally good. Behold his countenance: clear and warm, richly refined. The beauty of central virtue within, pervaded by coherent principle, thereby finds full expression. Within the utmost gravity dwells the utmost harmony; within his approachability remains something awe-inspiring. Thus centrality and harmony emerge at the proper times, unencumbered by selfish partiality; solemnity and concord shine together, completely effacing the traces of deliberate self-restraint. When education is accomplished to this degree, is not the Way of rites and music great indeed! It is fitting that the Three Kings invariably used it to educate their heirs apparent.

Yet is this all? The Grand Mentor, Junior Mentor, Preceptor, Guardian, Adviser, and Assistant—those to his left and right, before and behind, must all be upright men. In going out and coming in, rising and resting, he must follow only the correct Way. Only then can instruction be understood and virtue perfected. Thus earlier Confucian scholars said that the enduring security of the ancestral temples, the altars of state, and the people depends solely on assisting and nurturing the ruler’s virtue, so that he does not stray even half a step from upright men. Rites and music are indeed the great foundations of education; but beginning instruction early and carefully selecting those around the heir are also urgent tasks in nurturing him.

“When love is brought to its utmost, they are present; when sincerity is brought to its utmost, they become manifest. Manifest and present, they are never forgotten in the heart. How, then, could one fail to be reverent?”

Zhao Yongxian

先王之祭也心切於親而敬自不能已焉蓋心
切於親則親固在吾心矣如此而祭之敬豈容
已哉記祭義者蓋謂先王之祀親也聲色志欲
之常存而形容音響之昭著是誠有以異於人
者然果何以得此乎誠以祀親者其孰無愛然
不能無遺愛也先王致其愛焉而戀慕之極其
===
至是以恍惚之中有親存焉非真存也愛之所
結也亦孰無愨然不能無遺愨也先王致其愨
焉而敬謹之無以加是以彷佛之間有親著焉
非真著也愨之所感也夫著由於愨非暫著而
已愨不已則其著亦無已矣存由於愛非暫存
而已愛罔休則其存亦罔休矣若此而祭安得
不敬乎蓋人以親為不可見也故怠心生矣今
既著存不忘乎心則是其事死也猶事生也寧
有事之如生而敢怠焉者乎其事亡也猶事存

先王之祭也，心切於親，而敬自不能已焉。蓋心切於親，則親固在吾心矣。如此而祭之，敬豈容已哉？記祭義者蓋謂先王之祀親也，聲色志欲之常存，而形容音響之昭著，是誠有以異於人者。然果何以得此乎？誠以祀親者，其孰無愛？然不能無遺愛也。先王致其愛焉，而戀慕之極其至，是以恍惚之中有親存焉。非真存也，愛之所結也。亦孰無愨？然不能無遺愨也。先王致其愨焉，而敬謹之無以加，是以彷佛之間有親著焉。非真著也，愨之所感也。夫著由於愨，非暫著而已；愨不已，則其著亦無已矣。存由於愛，非暫存而已；愛罔休，則其存亦罔休矣。若此而祭，安得不敬乎？蓋人以親為不可見也，故怠心生矣。今既著存不忘乎心，則是其事死也猶事生也，寧有事之如生而敢怠焉者乎？其事亡也猶事存

Associate Examiner Shen, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: 〔“Thoughtful conception and forceful writing.”〕
Examiner Lü, Academician, comments: 〔“Clear understanding.”〕
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: 〔“Intimate and meaningful.”〕
When the former kings offered sacrifice, their hearts were deeply attached to their parents, and their reverence naturally could not cease. For when one’s heart is deeply attached to one’s parents, those parents are already present within one’s heart. Offering sacrifice in this state, how could one’s reverence cease? The author of “The Meaning of Sacrifices” meant that, when the former kings sacrificed to their parents, their parents’ voices, expressions, intentions, and desires remained constantly with them, while their forms and the sounds of their voices appeared distinctly. In this they truly differed from other people. But how did they attain this?
Among those who sacrifice to their parents, who lacks love? Yet their love cannot be without omissions. The former kings brought their love to its fullest extent, carrying their longing and yearning to the utmost; thus, amid indistinct impressions, their parents were present. They were not actually present: this was what concentrated love brought forth. Likewise, who lacks sincerity? Yet their sincerity cannot be without omissions. The former kings brought their sincerity to its fullest extent, so that nothing could be added to their reverent care; thus, amid faint semblances, their parents became manifest. They were not actually manifest: this was what sincerity called forth.
Their becoming manifest arose from sincerity, and was not merely momentary. As sincerity did not cease, neither did their manifestation. Their presence arose from love, and was not merely momentary. As love never rested, neither did their presence. Offering sacrifice in this state, how could one fail to be reverent? People suppose that their parents can no longer be seen, and so negligence arises in their hearts. But now, with their parents manifest and present, never forgotten in their hearts, they serve the dead just as they served the living. Could anyone serve them as though alive and yet dare to be negligent? They serve the departed just as they served those still present…

…Would anyone who serves them as though they were still present dare to be negligent? The intensity of sorrow stirs within the heart, and sincere reverence manifests itself in the countenance. This is no pretense: it cannot be otherwise. The rising sacrificial vapors touch the senses from without, and the resolve to perform the service reverently stirs within. This is not forced: it cannot be restrained. Ah! Such were the sacrifices of the former kings. Is this offering to one's parents the exclusive province of filial sons? Nevertheless, although sincerity is indeed prized in serving the spirits, how could one fully express love and earnestness at the time of sacrifice unless benevolence and filial devotion had long been cultivated in everyday life? Thus, although the sacrifice is the same, it was King Wen who cherished the thought of making seasonal offerings, and Confucius who felt the spirits to be present. Do those who stand unevenly and lean while attending a sacrifice not wish to be reverent? They simply lack the requisite character and therefore cannot be reverent. Should not those who would learn well from the sages likewise seek the foundation in their habitual conduct?

text:
同考試官編修李批詞意剴切摯然可備以為君德助矣
同考試官編修王批發明下民愛君之意警切明暢
詞復古雅文有識有養之士

此制藝鑿鑿皆實非豪語也

宜高薦
考試官大學士張批義意懇切詞旨微婉蓋素抱忠
愛之忱者首薦允宜
===
天之立君以為民也人君明於天之意則所以
自愛其身者必不輕矣夫以天下之大林林總
總之眾而無君則孰與治之人主以其身託於
天下君王之上而無民則孰與守之故世之愛
戴人主也莫不願其安富尊榮而長為君者非
獨愛其君也有之以為利故也人主之自愛其
身也亦莫不欲其壽考寧固而長為君者非獨
愛其身也有之以為天下利故也故貴以其身
為天下者乃可以託天下愛以其身為天下者

天之立君以爲民也人君明於天之意則所以
自愛其身者必不輕矣夫以天下之大林林總
總之衆而無君則孰與治之人主以其身託於
天下君王之上而無民則孰與守之故世之愛
戴人主也莫不願其安富尊榮而長爲君者非
獨愛其君也有之以爲利故也人主之自愛其
身也亦莫不欲其壽考寧固而長爲君者非獨
愛其身也有之以爲天下利故也故貴以其身
爲天下者乃可以託天下愛以其身爲天下者
punctuated:
同考試官編修李批：詞意剴切，摯然可備以為君德助矣。

同考試官編修王批：發明下民愛君之意，警切明暢，詞復古雅，文有識有養之士。

天之立君，以為民也。人君明於天之意，則所以自愛其身者必不輕矣。夫以天下之大，林林總總之眾，而無君，則孰與治之？人主以其身託於天下君王之上，而無民，則孰與守之？故世之愛戴人主也，莫不願其安富尊榮而長為君者，非獨愛其君也，有之以為利故也。人主之自愛其身也，亦莫不欲其壽考寧固而長為君者，非獨愛其身也，有之以為天下利故也。故貴以其身為天下者，乃可以託天下；愛以其身為天下者

Associate Examiner Li, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: The language and meaning are incisive and earnest. In its sincerity, this may serve to assist the ruler’s virtue.

Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: It elucidates the common people’s love for their ruler with admonitory force and lucid expression. Its language is also classically elegant—the writing of a man of discernment and cultivated character [?].

Associate Examiner Chen, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: Every passage discussing the ruler’s care for his own person is measured and appropriate. In this examination essay, every assertion is firmly grounded in reality; these are no grandiose words.

Examiner Lü, a Hanlin Academician, comments: His arguments are upright and broad in scope; his learning and discernment are extensive and profound. He is a man of cultivated character and fully deserves recommendation at a high rank.

Examiner Zhang, a Grand Secretary, comments: The ideas are earnest, and the language and purport subtle and tactful. He is evidently someone who has long cherished sincere loyalty and affection for his ruler. Recommendation in first place is entirely fitting.

Heaven establishes rulers for the sake of the people. If a ruler understands Heaven’s intention, he will surely not take lightly the care of his own person. Given the vastness of all under Heaven and its teeming multitudes, who would govern them if there were no ruler? The ruler entrusts his own person to a position above the kings of all under Heaven [?]; but if there were no people, who would safeguard him? Thus, when people love and revere their ruler, all wish him peace, wealth, honor, and glory, and wish him long to remain their ruler. This is not solely because they love their ruler, but because having him brings them benefit. Likewise, in caring for his own person, the ruler invariably desires longevity, peace, and security, and wishes long to remain ruler. This is not solely because he loves his own person, but because his continued presence benefits all under Heaven. Thus, one who values his own person in governing all under Heaven may be entrusted with all under Heaven; one who cherishes his own person in governing all under Heaven …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
乃可以保天下善乎宋儒魏氏之言曰人主保
身以保民蓋言人君子民之道也而愚又推之
于天今夫父母之于子也上以屬宗祊之重而
下以為昌後之圖也故其愛之也甚殷而憂之
也甚切勞之以其所不堪而約之使弗納於邪
其為子者亦舉足出言而不敢忘焉惟恐一旦
以其身之虧辱為父母憂故子之愛其身也非
以自為也體父母之愛為久遠計也大君者吾
父母宗子也又天之所甚愛者也賦之以聰明
===
聖智之資而畀之以崇高富貴之實使天下曽
不得睨視而跂望焉佐之以侯王君公之長而
授之以禮樂征伐之權使天下曽不得矯命而
雄行焉其愛之甚何也以為民也天下有强掩
弱衆暴寡懷知而不以相教擅利而不以相分
絶國殊俗僻遠幽遐不能以被德承澤然後舉
天下而授之一人號曰天子使之齊一其亂而
均適其欲衣食其饑寒而拊循其疾苦然後天
之意有所寄焉故人主之身非一人之身億萬

均適其欲衣食其饑寒而拊循其疾苦然後天
之意有所寄焉故人主之身非一人之身億萬

乃可以保天下。善乎宋儒魏氏之言曰：「人主保身以保民。」蓋言人君子民之道也。而愚又推之于天。今夫父母之于子也，上以屬宗祊之重，而下以為昌後之圖也。故其愛之也甚殷，而憂之也甚切，勞之以其所不堪，而約之使弗納於邪。其為子者，亦舉足出言而不敢忘焉，惟恐一旦以其身之虧辱為父母憂。故子之愛其身也，非以自為也，體父母之愛，為久遠計也。

大君者，吾父母宗子也，又天之所甚愛者也。賦之以聰明聖智之資，而畀之以崇高富貴之實，使天下曽不得睨視而跂望焉；佐之以侯王君公之長，而授之以禮樂征伐之權，使天下曽不得矯命而雄行焉。其愛之甚，何也？以為民也。天下有强掩弱，衆暴寡，懷知而不以相教，擅利而不以相分；絶國殊俗，僻遠幽遐，不能以被德承澤。然後舉天下而授之一人，號曰天子，使之齊一其亂而均適其欲，衣食其饑寒而拊循其疾苦，然後天之意有所寄焉。故人主之身，非一人之身，億萬
translation_en:
…only then can he preserve all under Heaven. Well said are the words of the Song Confucian scholar Wei: “The ruler preserves himself in order to preserve the people.” These words speak of the way a ruler cares for the people as his children. Yet I venture to extend this reasoning to Heaven. Parents entrust their son with the weighty responsibility of maintaining the ancestral temple above, and look to him to ensure the flourishing of their descendants below. Thus their love for him is profound and their concern for him acute. They make him toil at what he can scarcely endure and restrain him from falling into evil. The son, in turn, dares not forget them whenever he takes a step or utters a word, fearing only that some injury or disgrace to himself might one day cause his parents sorrow. Thus a son cherishes himself not for his own sake: he takes his parents’ love to heart and plans for the long future.

The great sovereign is our parent and the principal heir of our lineage, and is also deeply loved by Heaven. Heaven endows him with intelligence and sagely wisdom and grants him lofty status, wealth, and honor, so that none under Heaven can so much as look askance at him or stand on tiptoe in hopes of reaching his position. It gives him the leaders among the feudal lords as his assistants and entrusts him with authority over rites, music, and punitive expeditions, so that none under Heaven can presume to falsify his commands and act imperiously. Why does Heaven love him so deeply? For the sake of the people. In the world, the strong overwhelm the weak and the many oppress the few; those possessing knowledge do not use it to teach others, and those monopolizing benefits do not share them. Distant countries with differing customs, secluded and remote regions, cannot receive the influence of virtue and the bounty of beneficence. Heaven therefore takes all under Heaven and entrusts it to one man, naming him the Son of Heaven, so that he may bring order and unity to its disorder, satisfy its people’s desires equitably, clothe and feed the cold and hungry, and comfort and care for those suffering hardship. Only then does Heaven’s purpose have someone to whom it can be entrusted. Thus the ruler’s person is not the person of one man, but of the countless millions…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
兆人之身也天以民之故而愛君而人主不思
愛其身以保民則無乃孤天所以付託之意乎
然而人主之愛其身也與衆庶異不可不察也
庶民之愛其身也常患無以養之人主之愛其
身也常患無以制之何也凡人之情有不得則
其欲有節而用不窮無不得則其欲易恣而反
至於困憊人主之於天下也奚不得哉其威足
以怵惕其勢足以奔走可致之欲交於前而可
畏之機伏於後始於娛樂終於憂患而民與身
===
始交病矣明主知其然故常有以節之黼黻文
章所以養目也而冕旒蔽之不極其觀鐘鼓管
磬所以養耳也而黈纊塞之不淫於聰八珎在
御側載臭茝所以養口也而一餐告飽不求其
餘深宫曲房筦簟緹帷所以養體也而應門擊
柝鼓人上堂女史授環彤管紀過不求其娛負
扆以居勾陳營衞所以養安也而蟲飛會盈辨
色眡朝日中考政日昃不遑不求其便張官置
吏建侯樹屏所以養尊也而疑丞後先卜筮左

兆人之身也。天以民之故而愛君，而人主不思愛其身以保民，則無乃孤天所以付託之意乎？然而人主之愛其身也，與衆庶異，不可不察也。庶民之愛其身也，常患無以養之；人主之愛其身也，常患無以制之。何也？凡人之情，有不得則其欲有節而用不窮；無不得則其欲易恣而反至於困憊。人主之於天下也，奚不得哉？其威足以怵惕，其勢足以奔走。可致之欲交於前，而可畏之機伏於後；始於娛樂，終於憂患，而民與身始交病矣。
明主知其然，故常有以節之。黼黻文章，所以養目也，而冕旒蔽之，不極其觀；鐘鼓管磬，所以養耳也，而黈纊塞之，不淫於聰；八珎在御，側載臭茝，所以養口也，而一餐告飽，不求其餘；深宫曲房，筦簟緹帷，所以養體也，而應門擊柝，鼓人上堂，女史授環，彤管紀過，不求其娛；負扆以居，勾陳營衞，所以養安也，而蟲飛會盈，辨色眡朝，日中考政，日昃不遑，不求其便；張官置吏，建侯樹屏，所以養尊也，而疑丞後先，卜筮左
translation_en:
…the person of the countless multitudes. Heaven cherishes the ruler for the people's sake. If the ruler does not consider how to cherish his own person in order to protect the people, would he not betray Heaven's intention in entrusting him with this charge? Yet the way a ruler cherishes his person differs from that of ordinary people: this distinction must be examined. Ordinary people, in cherishing their persons, constantly worry that they lack the means to sustain themselves; a ruler, in cherishing his person, constantly worries that he lacks the means to restrain himself. Why? Human nature is such that, when some things remain beyond one's reach, desires have limits and resources are not exhausted. When nothing is beyond one's reach, desires readily become unbridled and ultimately lead instead to distress and exhaustion. What in all the world is beyond a ruler's reach? His majesty suffices to inspire fear, and his power to send others hurrying to obey. Attainable objects of desire crowd before him, while fearful dangers lie hidden behind. What begins in pleasure ends in anxiety and trouble, until both the people and the ruler himself suffer together.
An enlightened ruler understands this and therefore always has means of imposing restraint. Embroidered axe patterns and other ornamental designs nourish his eyes, yet the pendant beads of his ceremonial cap screen them, so that he does not indulge his sight to the utmost. Bells, drums, pipes, and chime stones nourish his ears, yet yellow floss ear pendants block them, so that he does not indulge excessively in listening. The eight delicacies are served before him, with fragrant angelica set beside them [?], to nourish his palate; yet after one meal he declares himself satisfied and seeks no more. Inner palaces and secluded chambers, rush and bamboo mats and reddish silk curtains, nourish his body; yet watchmen strike clappers at the principal palace gate, drummers ascend the hall, female scribes present rings, and vermilion brushes record his faults, so that he does not pursue pleasure. He sits with a ceremonial screen behind him, surrounded by an encircling guard, to provide for his security; yet “insects fly and the assembly fills” [?], he holds court as soon as colors can be distinguished at dawn, examines government affairs at midday, and has no leisure even as the sun declines, so that he does not seek his own ease. The establishment of offices and appointment of officials, the enfeoffment of lords and creation of protective bulwarks, sustain his exalted position; yet counselors and assistants attend behind and before him, and divination by turtle shell and milfoil stands to his left…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
右太史奉諱工師誦詩御瞽幾聲士庶傳謗不
求其徇禮樂刑政整齊約束所以養威也而虞
賓在位三恪助祭夏士在庭殷士在廟讎民在
甸夷隸在門不求其同凡所以養之者必有所
制不得極欲譬之百官有司事有所禀不得專
命若然者豈故拘攣齪齪屈萬乘而躬韋布之
行哉其節之者正所以愛之也夫物也者所以
養性也非以性養也以性徇物養生者慎之而
況於人主乎是以古之帝王善保其身者使欲
===
不窮於物物不屈於欲則其欲節矣欲有節則
神定神定則無越思欲有節則氣完氣完則無
過動欲有節則事簡事簡則無濫費是以慆心
溢志之事不滑其和而煩擾掊克之政不逮於
下精爽通於天地而德澤洽於寰宇含生之倫
仰上之德象主之指各便其性安其居處其宜
爲其能三光明六符正羣生遂長五穀蕃殖海
隅日出之邦雕題鑿齒之民莫不重譯貢琛歛
衽稽顙以戴天子天子者端委恭已而南面焉

punctuated: 右，太史奉諱，工師誦詩，御瞽幾聲，士庶傳謗，不求其徇。禮樂刑政，整齊約束，所以養威也；而虞賓在位，三恪助祭，夏士在庭，殷士在廟，讎民在甸，夷隸在門，不求其同。凡所以養之者，必有所制，不得極欲。譬之百官有司，事有所禀，不得專命。若然者，豈故拘攣齪齪，屈萬乘而躬韋布之行哉？其節之者，正所以愛之也。夫物也者，所以養性也，非以性養也。以性徇物，養生者慎之，而況於人主乎？是以古之帝王善保其身者，使欲不窮於物，物不屈於欲，則其欲節矣。欲有節則神定，神定則無越思；欲有節則氣完，氣完則無過動；欲有節則事簡，事簡則無濫費。是以慆心溢志之事不滑其和，而煩擾掊克之政不逮於下。精爽通於天地，而德澤洽於寰宇。含生之倫，仰上之德，象主之指，各便其性，安其居，處其宜，爲其能。三光明，六符正，羣生遂長，五穀蕃殖。海隅日出之邦，雕題鑿齒之民，莫不重譯貢琛，歛衽稽顙，以戴天子。天子者，端委恭已而南面焉。
translation_en:
…on the right; the Grand Astrologer presents the names to be avoided, the master musicians recite poems, the attending blind musicians offer admonition through music, and officials and commoners convey criticisms: he does not seek their acquiescence. Ritual, music, punishments, and government, with their ordering and restraints, serve to sustain his authority. Yet the descendant of Yu occupies his place as an honored guest, the descendants of three former dynasties assist at sacrifices, men of Xia stand in the court, men of Yin attend in the ancestral temple, people of hostile allegiance dwell in the royal domain, and foreign bondsmen serve at the gates: he does not seek to make them all alike. Everything that sustains him must have some restraint, so that his desires cannot reach their utmost extent. This is like the officials of the various offices: in their affairs they must receive instructions and cannot issue commands on their own authority. Is this deliberately to impose petty, cramping restrictions, lowering the lord of ten thousand chariots to practice the conduct of a commoner clothed in plain cloth? The very restraints placed upon him are precisely the means of cherishing him.

Material things serve to nourish one’s nature; one’s nature is not meant to nourish them. Those who nurture life take care not to sacrifice their nature to material things. How much more should the ruler of men do so! Thus the emperors and kings of antiquity who were skilled at preserving themselves ensured that their desires did not exhaust material resources and that material resources were not depleted by their desires. Their desires were thereby moderated. When desires are moderated, the spirit is settled; when the spirit is settled, there are no excessive thoughts. When desires are moderated, vital energy remains whole; when vital energy remains whole, there are no excessive actions. When desires are moderated, affairs are few; when affairs are few, there is no extravagant expenditure. Thus things that lead the heart into indulgence and the will into excess do not disturb his harmony, and vexatious, exploitative policies do not reach those below. His vital spirit communicates with Heaven and Earth, and his beneficence extends throughout the world.

All living beings look up to the virtue of their superior and follow their ruler’s intent, each finding ease in its nature, security in its dwelling, its proper place, and scope for its abilities. The three celestial luminaries shine brightly, the six celestial indicators are correctly aligned, all living things grow to maturity, and the five grains flourish and multiply. The lands at the ocean’s edge where the sun rises, and the peoples who tattoo their foreheads and file their teeth, all come through successive interpreters to offer precious tribute, gather up their robes, and bow their foreheads to the ground in homage to the Son of Heaven. The Son of Heaven, wearing ceremonial robes and cap and holding himself reverently, faces south upon his throne…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
澹然無爲寂然無聲而萬幾咸理矣中心悅愷
四體康豫而壽考且寧矣故古之盛帝明王在
位久者皆度世百千萬歲而不化其民就之如
日望之如雲愛之如父母而歸之如流水矯手
頓足謹呼祝頌欲萬世而爲君者豈非保身以
保民之明驗歟晚近世則不然以天下之大奉
一人之身而常苦其不足口厭甘脆而天下始
有藜藿不飽者矣身厭紈綺而天下始有短褐
不完者矣居厭廣麗而天下始有宵啼露處者
===
矣其弊至於離志解體而不可收拾則漢唐宋
之季世是已嗟乎彼其身之不保而又何以保
民乎哉夫彼之愛其身也亦無以異於古之帝
王而成敗相反榮辱異趨者古之帝王以養之
之道愛之也而彼以戕之之道愛之也故事有
順而相賊反而相成美疢之滋毒不若藥石之
生我也柔曼之傾意不若奇醜之益德也是以
明主不以天之所愛爲樂而以命之靡常爲懼
不以天下奉其身而以其身爲天下使其身常

punctuated: 澹然無爲，寂然無聲，而萬幾咸理矣；中心悅愷，四體康豫，而壽考且寧矣。故古之盛帝明王，在位久者，皆度世百千萬歲而不化。其民就之如日，望之如雲，愛之如父母，而歸之如流水，矯手頓足，謹呼祝頌，欲萬世而爲君者，豈非保身以保民之明驗歟？晚近世則不然，以天下之大奉一人之身，而常苦其不足。口厭甘脆，而天下始有藜藿不飽者矣；身厭紈綺，而天下始有短褐不完者矣；居厭廣麗，而天下始有宵啼露處者矣。其弊至於離志解體而不可收拾，則漢唐宋之季世是已。嗟乎！彼其身之不保，而又何以保民乎哉？夫彼之愛其身也，亦無以異於古之帝王，而成敗相反、榮辱異趨者，古之帝王以養之之道愛之也，而彼以戕之之道愛之也。故事有順而相賊、反而相成。美疢之滋毒，不若藥石之生我也；柔曼之傾意，不若奇醜之益德也。是以明主不以天之所愛爲樂，而以命之靡常爲懼；不以天下奉其身，而以其身爲天下，使其身常
translation_en:
…Serene in nonaction and still without a sound, he brings the myriad affairs of government into order. His heart is joyful, his limbs healthy and at ease, and he enjoys longevity and peace. Thus the great emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity who long occupied the throne all passed through hundreds, thousands, and myriads of years without changing [?]. Their people approached them as they would the sun, looked to them as they would clouds, loved them as parents, and flowed toward them like running water. Raising their hands and stamping their feet, they respectfully cried out blessings and praises, wishing them to remain their rulers for ten thousand generations. Is this not clear proof that preserving oneself serves to preserve the people?

In more recent times, things have been otherwise. The whole vast realm is made to support a single person, yet he constantly suffers from a sense of insufficiency. His palate tires of sweet and delicate foods, while people in the realm begin to lack even enough wild greens to fill their bellies. His body tires of fine silks, while people begin to lack even intact garments of coarse cloth. He tires of spacious and magnificent dwellings, while people begin to weep at night and sleep exposed to the elements. These abuses ultimately estrange people’s hearts and dissolve their bonds beyond repair: the closing years of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties were precisely like this. Alas! If such rulers cannot preserve themselves, how can they preserve the people?

Their love of themselves is no different from that of the emperors and kings of antiquity. Yet their success and failure are opposite, and their paths lead respectively to honor and disgrace, because the ancient emperors and kings loved themselves through practices that nurtured them, whereas these rulers loved themselves through practices that destroyed them. Thus some things gratify yet harm one another, while others oppose yet help one another. A pleasing ailment that breeds poison is inferior to medicines and healing stones that preserve my life; beguiling beauty that captivates the heart is inferior to extraordinary ugliness that strengthens virtue.

Therefore, an enlightened ruler takes no delight in being Heaven’s beloved, but fears the inconstancy of its mandate. He does not make the realm serve his person, but devotes his person to the realm, so that he himself always…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
有餘而無不足其民常安樂而無患誠以天之
愛我者甚殷而託之甚重故也嘗觀無逸一書
叙商周之哲王所以永壽命而配上帝者不外
乎抑畏恐懼卑服康功忠臣之愛君固如此也
而世乃有曰有天下而不以恣睢命之曰桎梏
嗟乎人主之欲保身以保民豈必若拘儒所云
神農憔悴堯瘦癯舜黧黑禹胼胝之爲勞哉又
豈必若術家所云吹噓呼吸吐故納新熊經鳥
伸鴟視虎顧之爲養哉惟不以天下與其心而
已不以天下與其心則内者不出而外者不入
内不出外不入則耳目聰明而心志寧一何事
之不節何功之不成而必曰以恣睢夫使人主
無常身而百姓無常保者必斯言矣抑愚聞之
爝火之方微也一指之所能息也及其燎原雖
江河之水弗能救矣鴻鵠之未孚也可俯而窺
也及其翺翔浮雲雖蒲且之巧弗能加矣人心
之欲其幾甚微而其究不可窮盖亦若此矣是
故善養心者貴豫主敬以存之典學以明之親

translation_en:
…has abundance and suffers no want, while his people remain at ease and free from affliction. This is truly because Heaven’s love for me is so profound, and the charge it entrusts to me so weighty. I have read the chapter “Against Idleness” (Wuyi), which recounts how the wise kings of Shang and Zhou prolonged their lives and became worthy counterparts of the Lord on High. Their means amounted to nothing beyond restraint, reverence and fear, humble dress, and work for the people’s well-being. Such indeed is a loyal minister’s love for his ruler. Yet there are those in the world who say: “To possess all under Heaven without indulging oneself at will is what we call being shackled.”

Alas! If a ruler wishes to preserve himself so as to preserve his people, must he necessarily toil as narrow-minded scholars describe—Shennong haggard, Yao emaciated, Shun darkened by exposure, and Yu callused on hands and feet? Or must he necessarily nourish himself in the ways described by practitioners of esoteric arts—breathing in and out, expelling the stale and taking in the fresh, hanging like a bear, stretching like a bird, staring like an owl, and looking back like a tiger? He need only refrain from surrendering his heart to the world. If he does not surrender his heart to the world, what is within will not go out, and what is outside will not enter. When the inner does not go out and the outer does not enter, his ears and eyes will be perceptive, and his heart and purpose tranquil and undivided. What affair would then lack due measure? What achievement would fail to be accomplished? Yet they insist on speaking of self-indulgence! Surely it is this saying that deprives rulers of lasting personal security and the common people of lasting protection.

Moreover, I, in my ignorance, have heard this: when a torch flame is still small, a single finger can extinguish it; once it sets the plain ablaze, even the waters of the Yangzi and Yellow Rivers cannot put it out. Before a wild swan has hatched, one can bend down and peer at it; once it soars among the floating clouds, even the skill of Pu Qie cannot reach it. The desires of the human heart are much like this: their first stirrings are exceedingly slight, but their ultimate extent is beyond reckoning. Thus those skilled in nourishing the heart prize taking precautions beforehand. They make reverence their guiding principle to preserve it, devote themselves to learning to illuminate it, and associate closely with …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
正人君子以維持之禁於未以制於未萌此豫
之道也所以保身保民者也
表

translation_en:
…upright men and gentlemen to sustain it; restraining it before it has…[?], and checking it before it sprouts: this is the way of taking precautions, whereby one preserves oneself and protects the people.

Memorial

A draft congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials, on the occasion when Wamosi of the Tang-period Huigu led his followers in submitting to the court, and an imperial decree ordered the Chief Minister Li Deyu to compose an Account of Allegiance from Foreign Lands and bestow it upon him. 〔Second year of Huichang〕

By Fang Yang.

Associate Examiner Wang, Acting Director, comments: “The submission of foreign peoples to the sovereign is a magnificent event, in antiquity as today. This composition expresses its praise in language that is classically elegant and conforms to the proper form. It should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Lu, Supervising Secretary of the Right, comments: “The language is dignified and elegant; in praising, it does not forget admonition. This is an accomplished example of four-and-six parallel prose.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Examining Editor, comments: “Its form is classically elegant, and its language richly ornamented. It should be recorded for transmission.”

Associate Examiner He, Hanlin Compiler, comments: “Its style is weighty and dignified, and its diction richly suggestive [?]. It can serve as a model.”

Examiner Lü, Academician, comments: “Within its praise it embeds admonition and indirect remonstrance. This is the work of someone sincerely intent on making a loyal offering. Accept it.”

Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “In praising, it does not forget admonition; it also displays devoted loyalty.”

In the fourth month of the second year of Huichang, Wamosi, chieftain of the Huigu, led his followers in submitting to the court. We have humbly received…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
聖慈嘉其誠欵封爲懷化郡王酋長徧加秩賞
特命宰臣撰異域歸忠傳賜之遠夷來格邊境
輯寧臣等誠懽誠忭稽首頓首稱
賀者伏以
聖主中興九譯戴同文之治名王内附十行承
賜札之恩仰
舜德以咸賓誦
堯言而不忒聲施蠻貊歡動寰區竊惟聖人以
六合爲家則邇者安遠者至天子以四夷
===
爲守則要服貢荒服王嘉靖殷邦爰致氐
羌之享丕單武烈聿來肅愼之庭凡雕題
漆齒之氓盡圖王會若辮髮貫胸之長咸
隷象胥盖上仁所不懷必至誠爲能化惟
茲回鶻世長北蕃樹牙乘突厥之衰通道
值貞觀之盛燕然請吏人羊竊比于中華
靈武徵兵蛇豕荐窺乎上國洎葉護狃東
都之勝致懷恩勾朔漠之師金繒和親不
解南侵之禍邊城互市竟渝北面之盟烽

六合爲家則邇者安遠者至天子以四夷

爲守則要服貢荒服王嘉靖殷邦爰致氐
羌之享丕單武烈聿來肅慎之庭凡雕題
漆齒之氓盡圖王會若辮髮貫胷之長咸
隷象胥蓋上仁所不懐必至誠爲能化惟
茲回鶻世長北蕃樹牙乘突厥之衰通道
值貞觀之盛燕然請吏入羊竊比于中華
靈武徵兵虵豕荐窺乎上國洎葉護伊東
都之勝致懐恩勾朔漠之師金繒和親不
解南侵之禍邊城互市竟渝北面之盟烽
punctuated:
聖慈嘉其誠欵，封爲懷化郡王，酋長徧加秩賞，特命宰臣撰《異域歸忠傳》賜之。遠夷來格，邊境輯寧，臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首稱賀者。伏以聖主中興，九譯戴同文之治；名王内附，十行承賜札之恩。仰舜德以咸賓，誦堯言而不忒。聲施蠻貊，歡動寰區。

竊惟聖人以六合爲家，則邇者安、遠者至；天子以四夷爲守，則要服貢、荒服王。嘉靖殷邦，爰致氐羌之享；丕單武烈，聿來肅愼之庭。凡雕題漆齒之氓，盡圖王會；若辮髮貫胸之長，咸隷象胥。盖上仁所不懷，必至誠爲能化。

惟茲回鶻，世長北蕃。樹牙乘突厥之衰，通道值貞觀之盛。燕然請吏，人羊竊比于中華；靈武徵兵，蛇豕荐窺乎上國。洎葉護狃東都之勝，致懷恩勾朔漠之師。金繒和親，不解南侵之禍；邊城互市，竟渝北面之盟。烽
translation_en:
…Your Majesty graciously commended his sincerity and invested him as Prince of Huaihua Commandery. Ranks and rewards were bestowed upon all the chieftains, and the chief ministers were specially commanded to compose an Account of Allegiance from Foreign Lands and present it to him. Distant foreigners have come in submission, and the frontier is tranquil. We, your servants, in true joy and delight, bow our heads to the ground and kowtow to offer congratulations. We humbly reflect: as our sagely sovereign restores the dynasty’s greatness, peoples requiring nine successive interpreters embrace a rule under which all share one written language; as an illustrious foreign king submits, he receives the gracious gift of an imperial letter in ten lines. Looking up to virtue like Shun’s, all come as guests; reciting words like Yao’s, they do not stray. Your renown spreads among the Man and Mo peoples, and joy stirs the entire realm.

We humbly consider that when the sage makes the six directions his home, those nearby dwell in peace and those far away arrive; when the Son of Heaven makes the peoples of the four quarters his defenders, the outer submission zone brings tribute and the remote wilderness zone acknowledges his kingship. Bringing good order and peace to the lands of Yin thus drew offerings from the Di and Qiang; fully displaying martial achievements brought the Sushen to court. All the people with tattooed foreheads and blackened teeth were depicted in the Assembly of Kings; chieftains with braided hair or pierced chests were all placed under the interpreter officials. For those whom supreme benevolence does not win over [?], only utter sincerity can bring transformation.

Now these Huihu have for generations held sway over the northern border peoples. They raised their standards as the Tujue declined and opened communications during the flourishing Zhenguan era. At Yanran they requested officials: these sheep-like people presumptuously compared themselves with the people of the Central Realm. When troops were summoned at Lingwu, these snakes and swine repeatedly cast covetous eyes upon the sovereign realm. Then the yabghu, emboldened by victory at the Eastern Capital, brought about Huaien’s summoning of troops from the northern desert. Gold and silk and marriage alliances did not end the scourge of southward incursions; despite mutual trade in the frontier cities, they ultimately broke their covenant of submission as subjects. Beacon fires…

車駕頻煩于細柳屬關隴腥羶之後徒事羈縻
當藩臣跋扈之秋未遑經略百年胡運尚
寬膏斧之誅一統

translation_en:
…smoke from the beacon fires repeatedly reached Ganquan, and the imperial carriage was frequently troubled to journey to Xiliu. After the lands of Guan and Long had been tainted by the rank stench of the invaders, the court did no more than maintain loose control; in an age when feudatory ministers acted without restraint, it had no leisure for strategic governance. Through a hundred years of barbarian ascendancy, punishment beneath the executioner's axe was still withheld; now, with the imperial realm united, we suddenly behold a gathering to present precious tribute.

This, we humbly submit, is because we have encountered 〇〇〇〇: Your Majesty is endowed with sagely discernment, and Heaven has bestowed courage and wisdom upon you. Letting your robes hang down, you govern without exertion, presiding over an age when the Yellow River runs clear and the seas are calm. Reverently wielding the battle-axe, you unleash the force of thunder's fury and flying winds. Seated in the Hall of Light, you receive the assembled lords in audience; bestowing kindness upon the Central Kingdom, you bring tranquillity to the four quarters. The Yuezhi don caps and girdles, together answering the auspicious appearance of the zouya beast; from the lands of sunrise, peoples cross mountains by ladders and seas by ships, all conveying precious ivory.

Your divine might reaches freely into the distant wilderness; your moral instruction spreads widely among peoples who speak through interpreters. Thus the descendants of the khagans come to court with cords bound about them in submission, and the great chieftains bearing the title tegin sheath their weapons and approach the frontier gates to offer allegiance. Jackals and wolves subdue their ferocious nature; owls cherish our kindly words. Although the disposition of the barbarians is inconstant in rebellion and submission, the nurturing reach of your sagely beneficence ultimately excludes none. Written pledges in cinnabar confer sworn assurances, already exalting the enfeoffment of the Rizhu king; red ceremonial knee-covers bestow distinction, further enhancing the reward of Zhizi [?]. This has further engaged…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
宸慮特詔台司裒武義貞烈之臣輯異域歸忠
之傳遠稽秦漢近採
皇唐始戎由余之見幾終尚可孤之著節寫諸
琬琰播狼胥瀚海之聲炳若丹青掩麟閣
雲臺之美袞鉞中嚴于筆削絲綸下逮于
兜離感以至誠喜溢淄青之詔陳之大訓
榮逾飛白之書俾觀古以知今用變夷而
之夏信王者懷柔之大德妙聖人鼓舞之
微權彼呼韓請朝特位侯王之上乃竇融
===
歸款遽蒙圖傳之頒然未有襲我冠裳為
王屏翰稽顙而臣闕下穹廬獲齒于內藩
推心以置腹中文字遂通于殊俗允矣
聖朝之盛事昭哉史冊之休光臣等材謝請纓
籌疎借箸元戎十乘期賡六月之詩干羽
兩階幸覩七旬之格瞻
龍顏而有喜爾虎拜以揚休伏願
居安慮危
柔遠能邇如天覆幬益隆下濟之謙未雨綢

歸欵遽蒙圖傳之須然未有襲我冠裳為
王屏翰稽顙而臣闕下穹廬獲齒于內藩
推心以置腹以文字遂通于殊俗允矣
聖朝之盛事昭哉史冊之休光臣等材謝請纓
籌疎借筯元戎十乘期賡六月之詩干羽
兩階幸覩七旬之格瞻
龍顏而有喜爾虎拜以揚休伏願
居安慮危
柔遠能邇如天覆幬益隆下濟之謙未兩綢
punctuated:
宸慮，特詔台司，裒武義貞烈之臣，輯異域歸忠之傳。遠稽秦漢，近採皇唐，始戎由余之見幾，終尚可孤之著節。寫諸琬琰，播狼胥瀚海之聲；炳若丹青，掩麟閣雲臺之美。袞鉞中嚴于筆削，絲綸下逮于兜離。感以至誠，喜溢淄青之詔；陳之大訓，榮逾飛白之書。俾觀古以知今，用變夷而之夏。信王者懷柔之大德，妙聖人鼓舞之微權。彼呼韓請朝，特位侯王之上；乃竇融歸款，遽蒙圖傳之頒。然未有襲我冠裳，為王屏翰，稽顙而臣闕下，穹廬獲齒于內藩；推心以置腹，中文字遂通于殊俗。允矣，聖朝之盛事；昭哉，史冊之休光！

臣等材謝請纓，籌疎借箸。元戎十乘，期賡《六月》之詩；干羽兩階，幸覩七旬之格。瞻龍顏而有喜，爾虎拜以揚休。伏願居安慮危，柔遠能邇，如天覆幬，益隆下濟之謙；未雨綢
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s concern, prompting a special decree to the highest ministers to gather accounts of men distinguished by martial righteousness, steadfastness, and devotion, and compile biographies of those from foreign lands who came over in loyalty. They searched far back into Qin and Han and drew on the more recent august Tang, beginning with the foresight of You Yu of the Rong and ending with the manifest fidelity of Shang Kegu. Inscribed upon precious stone, these accounts spread their renown to Langxu and the Hanhai; brilliant as painted portraits, they surpass the glory of the Qilin Pavilion and the Cloud Terrace. Within the court, praise and censure are rigorously apportioned through the historian’s recording and omission; abroad, imperial pronouncements reach even those who speak foreign tongues. Moved by utmost sincerity, their joy exceeds that expressed in the edict concerning Ziqing; set forth as a great admonition, their honor surpasses that conferred by an inscription in flying-white script. Thus, by contemplating antiquity, they may understand the present, and through transformation pass from the ways of the outsiders to those of the Chinese. Truly this is the sovereign’s great virtue of conciliating distant peoples, and the sage’s subtle skill in inspiring them.

When Huhan requested an audience, he was specially ranked above marquises and kings; when Dou Rong pledged allegiance, he promptly received an imperially bestowed illustrated biography. Yet never before have men adopted our caps and robes and become bulwarks of the throne, knocking their foreheads upon the ground and acknowledging themselves subjects beneath the palace gates, so that those dwelling in felt tents gained a place among the inner feudatories. Through trust that lays bare the heart, Chinese writing has thereby reached peoples of different customs. Truly, this is a grand achievement of the sagely dynasty; how resplendent its glory in the historical record!

We, Your servants, lack the talent to volunteer for a mission with a binding cord in hand, and our strategic judgment falls short of offering counsel with borrowed chopsticks. With ten great war chariots, we hope to continue the song of the “Sixth Month”; with shields and feather plumes displayed between the two stairways, we are fortunate to witness submission within seventy days. We look upon Your joyful imperial countenance and bow like Hu to proclaim Your glory. Prostrate, we pray that, dwelling in security, You will consider danger, conciliate those afar and bring harmony to those nearby. Sheltering all as Heaven does, may You further exalt the humility that reaches down to those below; before the rain, make preparations…

大臣等無任瞻
天仰

表稱

聞

策五道
第一問
史鈳
同考試官郎中呂批我

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
益章顯志弘業相須而共濟盛美溢乎當
世聲光流於無窮盖自唐虞以及
昭代致理之原古今一揆矣愚請繹泰之義
先著君臣之所以交然後鋪張我
祖
宗休烈可乎易天地交泰后以裁成天地之道
輔相天地之宜以左右民夫泰之言通也
后以裁成輔相爲事盖身視臣庶而家視
寰宇使元首與股肱弗相聯屬則精神不
===
貫而身病使主伯與亞旅弗相親比則意
氣不洽而家睽故天道下濟地道上行絪
縕訢合以生萬物交也者天地之所不能
違也而況於人乎人臣懷忠信之心抱匡
濟之畫孰不欲委質清時結心明主然而
冠履之分嚴而宫庭之地隔其情易渙而
其勢易疎也明主知其然故首出庶物而
下芻蕘兼制四海而先瞽御朝而議政坐
而論道所以優體也虚懷而聽造膝而籌

punctuated: 益章，顯志弘業，相須而共濟，盛美溢乎當世，聲光流於無窮。盖自唐虞以及昭代，致理之原，古今一揆矣。愚請繹泰之義，先著君臣之所以交，然後鋪張我祖宗休烈，可乎？《易》：「天地交，泰；后以裁成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。」夫泰之言，通也。后以裁成輔相爲事，盖身視臣庶而家視寰宇。使元首與股肱弗相聯屬，則精神不貫而身病；使主伯與亞旅弗相親比，則意氣不洽而家睽。故天道下濟，地道上行，絪縕訢合，以生萬物。交也者，天地之所不能違也，而況於人乎？人臣懷忠信之心，抱匡濟之畫，孰不欲委質清時，結心明主？然而冠履之分嚴，而宫庭之地隔，其情易渙，而其勢易疎也。明主知其然，故首出庶物而下芻蕘，兼制四海而先瞽。御朝而議政，坐而論道，所以優體也；虚懷而聽，造膝而籌，
translation_en:
…become still more illustrious; they manifest their purposes and enlarge their undertaking, relying upon one another to bring it to completion. Their splendid achievements abound in their own age, and their renown and glory endure without end. From the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun down to our illustrious dynasty, the source of good government has followed the same principle, ancient and modern alike. May I, in my humble judgment, unfold the meaning of Tai (Peace), first explaining how ruler and ministers establish intercourse, and then setting forth the glorious achievements of our imperial ancestors?

The Book of Changes says: “Heaven and earth interconnect: Peace. The sovereign accordingly shapes and completes the Way of heaven and earth, assists what is fitting to heaven and earth, and thereby guides and supports the people.” Tai means free communication. The sovereign makes shaping, completing, and assisting his task, regarding his ministers and common people as his own body, and the whole realm as his household. If the head and the limbs are not connected, the vital spirit cannot circulate and the body falls ill. If the household’s chief and its subordinate members [?] do not maintain close relations, their feelings and intentions will not harmonize, and the household will be divided. Thus the Way of heaven descends to aid below, and the Way of earth rises upward; their energies intertwine and unite harmoniously to bring forth all things. Intercourse is something that even heaven and earth cannot dispense with—how much less can human beings!

Ministers cherish loyal and trustworthy hearts and harbor plans to rectify affairs and bring aid. Who among them would not wish to pledge service in an age of enlightened government and bind his heart to an enlightened ruler? Yet the distinction between crown and footwear—that is, ruler and subject—is strict, and the palace precincts stand apart. Their feelings may readily become estranged, and their respective positions readily keep them distant. An enlightened ruler understands this. Hence, although he stands foremost among all beings, he humbles himself before grass-cutters and wood-gatherers; although he governs all within the Four Seas, he gives precedence to the blind musicians [?]. He presides at court to discuss government and sits with his ministers to discourse on the Way: these are means of treating them with generosity and consideration. He listens with an open mind, and they draw close to his knees to deliberate…

text:
所以致親也日晏侍食夜分徹炬所以示
渥也辟左右借顏色披衷愫忘忌諱所以
盡情也君資於內曰爾惟麴蘗爾惟鹽梅
臣順於外曰斯謀惟后斯猷惟后所以一
德也泰九二以剛中應五而六五柔中虛
己以從之此之謂君臣之交故泰之初拔
茅彙征與共開焉泰之極艱貞無咎與共
保焉二言所為五不言所為二臣道也以
任事為忠五君道也以任人為大二勝其
===
任則五可無為故曰以祉元吉而已此之
謂君臣交而為泰也夫都俞咨命喜起賡
歌唐虞尚矣三代相與載在詩書君臣之
情猶可想見由漢而下肇造元勳中興名
佐代固有之然率外合而中疑文具而情
閡建武數引公卿講論而責以吏事則其
體失也貞觀宰相入閤議事而隨以諫官
則其中疑也慶曆龍圖天章閤降手詔給
筆札而固辭不對則臣負其君也治平中

所以致親也。日晏侍食，夜分徹炬，所以示渥也。辟左右，借顏色，披衷愫，忘忌諱，所以盡情也。君資於內，曰：「爾惟麴蘗，爾惟鹽梅。」臣順於外，曰：「斯謀惟后，斯猷惟后。」所以一德也。泰九二以剛中應五，而六五柔中，虛己以從之，此之謂君臣之交。故泰之初，拔茅彙征，與共開焉；泰之極，艱貞無咎，與共保焉。二言所為，五不言所為。二，臣道也，以任事為忠；五，君道也，以任人為大。二勝其任，則五可無為，故曰：「以祉元吉」而已。此之謂君臣交而為泰也。

…these are the means of drawing them close. Having them attend him at meals late in the day, and removing the torches only at midnight, are means of showing generous favor. Dismissing his attendants, adopting a kindly expression, revealing his innermost feelings, and setting aside taboos are means of fully expressing his sentiments. The ruler relies upon them inwardly, saying, “You are my ferment and malt; you are my salt and sour plums.” The minister responds obediently in his outward conduct, saying, “These plans are all the sovereign’s; these counsels are all the sovereign’s.” These are the means of becoming united in virtue. In the hexagram Tai, Peace, the nine in the second place responds to the fifth through its strength and centrality, while the six in the fifth place, yielding and central, humbles itself to follow it. This is what is meant by communion between ruler and minister. Thus, at the beginning of Tai, “pulling up thatch grass” and “advancing together with its kind,” they jointly inaugurate peace; at the culmination of Tai, by “remaining steadfast amid difficulty, without blame,” they jointly preserve it. The second line speaks of what is done; the fifth does not. The second represents the way of the minister, whose loyalty consists in undertaking affairs; the fifth represents the way of the ruler, whose greatness consists in entrusting responsibilities to others. If the second fulfills its charge, the fifth can remain without action. Hence it says only, “Thereby attaining blessings: supremely auspicious.” This is what is meant by ruler and minister communing to bring about peace.
The exchanges of assent, consultation, and commands, and the responsive singing about rejoicing and rising to action, belong to the remote age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun. The mutual dealings of rulers and ministers under the Three Dynasties are recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, and their feelings toward one another can still be imagined. From the Han onward, every age certainly had founding men of great merit and renowned assistants in dynastic restoration. Yet for the most part they agreed outwardly while harboring doubts within; formalities were complete, but their feelings remained estranged. During the Jianwu reign, the emperor repeatedly summoned dukes and high ministers for discussion, yet held them accountable for clerical business: this violated the proper manner of treating them. During the Zhenguan reign, chief councilors entered the council chamber to deliberate on affairs, yet remonstrance officials were sent in after them: this showed inward distrust. During the Qingli reign, at the Longtu and Tianzhang Pavilions, the emperor issued an edict in his own hand and supplied brushes and writing materials, yet the ministers firmly declined to reply: here the ministers failed their ruler. …Sima Guang requested that the attendant officials be ordered to take turns on duty in the Zishan Hall and spend the night in the Chongwen Institute, awaiting an imperial summons. Yet this was never implemented: here the ruler failed his ministers. How could they hope to approach the flourishing harmony that comes from mutual intercourse? I have reverently read the opening chapter of the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao), “Ruler and Ministers Roam Together,” which states: “Throughout the dynasties, rulers and ministers have united their hearts and energies, established guiding principles and set forth regulations, proclaimed them throughout the realm, and brought blessings to the people. Thereby they moved Heaven and Earth, bringing seasonable weather, abundant harvests, and sufficiency to every household and person.” Great indeed is this sagely counsel! It was by following this way that our imperial ancestor and the successive sage emperors engaged with their ministers and made their eras flourish in peace. Allow me to outline this briefly.
Emperor Gao recruited outstanding and worthy men and pacified the Chinese realm. Among those with whom he shared confidential deliberations and who assisted his grand designs were Ji, Lian, An, Yi, Yi, Chen, and Yanliang. Emperor Wen personally honored eminent Confucian scholars and brought peace to the realm. Among those with whom he discussed critical affairs and who accompanied him on military campaigns were Jin, Guang, Huai, Yan, Rong, Shiqi, and Youzi. At the dynasty’s founding, when all was still unsettled and warfare allowed no respite, and amid the turmoil of strife within the imperial house, when recovery from devastation had only just begun, such was the relationship between ruler and ministers. Thus their spirits flowed together and their vital energies circulated freely, and the supreme harmony of Heaven and Earth extended…

及羣生，施於方外，而一代之鴻圖定矣。所謂開天地之泰者，非邪？

…reached all living beings and extended beyond the realm, and thus the dynasty’s grand design was established. Was this not what is meant by inaugurating the harmonious prosperity of Heaven and Earth?
Successive sage emperors inherited the throne, maintaining enduring peace and lasting good government. The Xuande and Hongzhi eras were especially celebrated as the height of prosperity. Emperor Zhang kept freedom from indolence in his heart and neglected none of the venerable senior ministers. Among the grand secretaries were Rong, Shiqi, and Pu; among the ministry officials were Yi, Yuanji, and Ying. He frequently summoned them for audiences in the Palace of Abstinence and his private halls. When touring the hills or boating, he bestowed compositions and provided meals. On one occasion he said, “Of one mind and one virtue, neither side harbors suspicion of the other”; on another, “In our excursions and recreation, may we approach the ways of antiquity.” How joyful and harmonious their relations were!
Emperor Jing aspired to great accomplishments, and seasoned ministers were all at hand. Among those directing government were Pu, Jian, Dongyang, and Qian; among the officials of the censorate and central administration were Wensheng, Daxia, and Shan. He frequently summoned them for audiences at the Platform and in the Warm Pavilion. His imperial countenance brightened, and deliberations on affairs of state were thorough and detailed. In draft memorials he would sometimes change a few characters or delete a few phrases; when ministers persisted in their representations, discussions might last for some time or even extend over several days. How open and unreserved their relations were! After generations of peace, when established laws and practices were firmly settled and affairs followed accustomed routines, complacency and negligence could easily arise. Yet such was the fellowship between ruler and ministers that spiritual influence flowed freely, vital energies circulated unhindered, and Heaven and Earth attained supreme harmony. Yao [?] …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
篤
前烈施于后昆而萬世之長策建矣所謂保天
地之泰者非邪當其時
主無貳任臣無隱忠懽忻交通而德威宣暢故
論開濟則功軼於姬姒頌熙洽則治匹于
唐虞而一時名臣碩輔幸逢
昌運亦得以勒勳德於旂常垂功名於竹帛
猗歟休哉真千載一時之遇也今
天子光撫鴻圖祇遵
===
成憲
講學臨政寒暑必親嘉言忠謨聽納靡倦公
卿百執事相與勵翼於下而
天子恭己南面以聽之內寧外謐時和年豐點
虜来庭炎荒奏凱斯亦泰運之再昌已而
執事尚欲聞保泰之說則愚將何詞以獻
乎竊以為欲登太平之理莫若致隆於上
下之交欲隆乎上下之交莫若憲章乎
召對之典夫人情狃於法之所常行而惕於意

今天子光撫鴻圖，祇遵成憲。講學臨政，寒暑必親；嘉言忠謨，聽納靡倦。公卿百執事，相與勵翼於下，而天子恭己南面以聽之。內寧外謐，時和年豐，點虜来庭，炎荒奏凱，斯亦泰運之再昌已。而執事尚欲聞保泰之說，則愚將何詞以獻乎？竊以為欲登太平之理，莫若致隆於上下之交；欲隆乎上下之交，莫若憲章乎召對之典。夫人情狃於法之所常行，而惕於意
translation_en:
…consolidated the achievements of his predecessors and extended their benefits to later generations, thereby establishing a lasting policy for ten thousand ages. Was this not what is meant by preserving the harmonious prosperity of Heaven and Earth? At that time, the sovereign entrusted his ministers with responsibility without wavering, and the ministers withheld none of their loyalty. They communicated joyfully and freely, and virtue and authority spread unhindered. Thus, in founding and sustaining the enterprise, his achievements surpassed those of the houses of Ji and Si; in flourishing harmony, his government rivaled those of Tang and Yu. The renowned ministers and eminent counselors of that age, fortunate enough to encounter such flourishing times, likewise had their meritorious virtue inscribed on ceremonial banners and their achievements and reputations transmitted in the historical records. Ah, how splendid! Truly this was an encounter seen but once in a thousand years!
Now the Son of Heaven gloriously presides over the great imperial enterprise and reverently follows established institutions. In heat and cold alike, he personally attends lectures and conducts government; he never tires of hearing and accepting worthy words and loyal counsel. The highest dignitaries and all officials together exert themselves in support below, while the Son of Heaven reverently composes himself and faces south to hear them. Within there is peace, and beyond the borders tranquility; the seasons are favorable and the harvests abundant. The barbarians [?] come to court, and victories are announced from the distant, torrid regions. This, too, is a renewed flourishing of an age of harmonious prosperity. Yet you still wish to hear how such prosperity may be preserved. What words, then, can I, in my ignorance, offer?
I humbly believe that to attain an age of great peace, nothing is better than strengthening communication between those above and those below; to strengthen that communication, nothing is better than following the established practice of summoning ministers for imperial consultation. For human nature grows accustomed to what regulations routinely prescribe, but is roused to vigilance by deliberate …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
之所間舉今辨色而入日出而
視之頃刻而退矣習則玩玩則不可振故不若
間一
召對之為益也盖有六善焉閱世務一也察材
品二也明德意三也密事幾四也定
國是五也激忠悃六也請得實以
祖
宗故事熟數于前而執事試垂聽焉夫人主雖
神聖睿智而四方庶務弗能周也錢穀刑
===
獄各有主者
召而問之則幽隱畢達故屯田鹽法欲計其宜
而臨淮洛陽得畢慮于下矣邊備虜情欲
定其算而鈞陽華容得决筴於前矣故以
閱世務則率作考成可弗眩也夫退而具
疏則詞可飾也思而陳訓則端可匿也惟
卒然問之心術立見能否莫逃故吕震與
儀智並對而諛直見楊士竒與蹇義並對
而遲敏見故以察材品則明闇回正可弗

punctuated:
之所間舉。今辨色而入，日出而視之，頃刻而退矣。習則玩，玩則不可振，故不若間一召對之為益也。盖有六善焉：閱世務，一也；察材品，二也；明德意，三也；密事幾，四也；定國是，五也；激忠悃，六也。請得實以祖宗故事，熟數于前，而執事試垂聽焉。
夫人主雖神聖睿智，而四方庶務弗能周也。錢穀刑獄，各有主者。召而問之，則幽隱畢達。故屯田鹽法欲計其宜，而臨淮、洛陽得畢慮于下矣；邊備虜情欲定其算，而鈞陽、華容得决筴於前矣。故以閱世務，則率作考成可弗眩也。
夫退而具疏，則詞可飾也；思而陳訓，則端可匿也。惟卒然問之，心術立見，能否莫逃。故吕震與儀智並對，而諛直見；楊士竒與蹇義並對，而遲敏見。故以察材品，則明闇回正可弗
translation_en:
…what is undertaken only occasionally. Nowadays, officials enter at the first light of dawn; at sunrise the ruler receives them, and in a moment they withdraw. Familiarity breeds heedlessness, and heedlessness makes it impossible to rouse them. Thus this is less beneficial than an occasional summons to an imperial audience. Such audiences have six merits: first, reviewing affairs of government; second, discerning ability and character; third, making the ruler’s virtuous intentions clear; fourth, handling incipient affairs discreetly; fifth, settling the direction of state policy; and sixth, inspiring heartfelt loyalty. Allow me to substantiate these points with precedents from our imperial ancestors, recounting them in detail before you; may you give them a hearing.
Though the ruler possesses sagely wisdom and penetrating intelligence, he cannot comprehend every detail of the many affairs throughout the realm. Revenue, grain, punishments, and judicial proceedings each have their responsible officials. Summon and question them, and even obscure and hidden matters will all be made known. Thus, when the suitability of military agricultural colonies and salt regulations was to be considered, the officials from Linhuai and Luoyang were able to lay out their deliberations fully before the throne. When plans concerning frontier defenses and the circumstances of the enemy were to be settled, the officials from Junyang and Huarong were able to determine strategies in the imperial presence. Thus, by reviewing affairs of government, the ruler can direct work and assess its results without confusion.
If officials withdraw and prepare memorials, their language can be embellished; if they deliberate before presenting counsel, their motives can be concealed. Only when questioned unexpectedly do their dispositions and intentions become immediately apparent, leaving their competence or incompetence nowhere to hide. Thus, when Lü Zhen and Yi Zhi answered together, their flattery and uprightness became apparent; when Yang Shiqi and Jian Yi answered together, their slowness and quickness became apparent. Thus, by discerning ability and character, intelligence and obtuseness, perversity and rectitude need not…

text:
欺也
上意猶的也射者爭趨之故諸司奏請必令稽
舊章侍臣以此知
上意之在守法
召問天下何時太平朕安得如古帝王大臣以
此知
上意之在興治誠以明
德意則措注嚮往可弗違也夫造膝而密語者
不可以先傳也從容而納誨者不可以瀆
===
盡也假令議廣
詔條而可令多人知乎出廠帖議改
命可外泄乎故以密事幾則轉移變化可弗窺
也衆議畢集可否易淆不惟憸夫與正士
殊科即君子意見亦有同異如移師彰德
楊榮以為是士奇以為非舉伏伯安為使
蹇義以為可原吉以為不可黎利請立陳
氏後張輔蹇夏曰勿許榮士奇曰許之此
其心皆體國而所見各殊惟析以

…be deceived.

The sovereign’s intent is like a target toward which archers vie to aim. Thus, when the various offices submitted requests, he invariably ordered them to consult established precedents; from this, his attendant officials knew that his intent was to uphold the laws. When he summoned his great ministers and asked, “When will All under Heaven enjoy peace? How can I become like the emperors and kings of antiquity?” they knew that his intent was to bring about good government. Truly, by making his beneficent intentions clear, he could ensure that their actions and aspirations did not run counter to them.

Words spoken confidentially at close quarters cannot be transmitted beforehand; counsel offered at leisure cannot all be divulged indiscriminately. Suppose they discussed expanding the provisions of an edict [?]: could many people be allowed to know? If a depot warrant were issued and they discussed changing the command [?], could this be leaked outside? Thus, by keeping incipient affairs secret, shifts and changes could be concealed from scrutiny.

===
眷顧迨今誦之猶爲感動况親當其盛者乎
故以激忠悃則銜恩幸遇可弗負也斯六
善者皆已事之明驗盖於法制常行之外
而時用吾鼓舞不測之權故
聖智日益觀聽日新賢才樂爲之用而天地常
泰且初雖似勞久而情誼洽彌見其適初
雖似煩久而要領得彌見其簡又何煩勞
之有愚又聞
punctuated:
宸衷，則衆論一矣。故以定國是，則盈庭聚訟可弗亂也。夫入侍帷幄，出奉乘輿，内寄腹心，外資謀斷，人人自以為親已矣。有君如此，其忍負之？祖宗朝親與盛事，藏在秘府，愚不得徧觀。即如泰和、長沙、華容之所私錄，毗倚眷顧，迄今誦之猶為感動，况親當其盛者乎？故以激忠悃，則銜恩幸遇可弗負也。

斯六善者，皆已事之明驗。蓋於法制常行之外，而時用吾鼓舞不測之權，故聖智日益，觀聽日新，賢才樂為之用，而天地常泰。且初雖似勞，久而情誼洽，彌見其適；初雖似煩，久而要領得，彌見其簡。又何煩勞之有？愚又聞
translation_en:
…through the sovereign’s judgment, the many opinions are unified. Thus, by settling the guiding policy of the state, one can prevent a court full of competing arguments from creating disorder. When ministers enter, they attend within the imperial chambers; when they go out, they accompany the imperial carriage. Inwardly, they are entrusted as confidants; outwardly, their counsel and decisions are relied upon. Each considers himself personally close to the ruler. With such a sovereign, how could they bear to fail him? Records of the splendid occasions of intimate association at the courts of the imperial ancestors [?] are preserved in the palace archives, and I have not been able to examine them all. Yet even the private records of Taihe, Changsha, and Huarong describe such reliance and gracious regard that reading them aloud still moves us today. How much more must this have been so for those who personally experienced those flourishing times? Thus, by inspiring heartfelt loyalty, one can ensure that those grateful for imperial favor and fortunate in their encounters with the ruler do not betray his trust.

These six benefits all have clear confirmation in past events. Beyond the regular operation of laws and institutions, the ruler from time to time exercises his unfathomable power to inspire and encourage. Thus his sagely wisdom increases daily, what he sees and hears is daily renewed, worthy and talented men gladly serve him, and Heaven and Earth remain in harmony. Moreover, although this may initially seem laborious, as mutual affection grows harmonious over time, its ease becomes increasingly apparent. Although it may initially seem troublesome, as the essential principles are grasped over time, its simplicity becomes increasingly apparent. What trouble or labor, then, is there? I have also heard…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
二祖諸臣皆從事乎草昧劬勩間而宣德弘治
所親禮乃其輔導之舊蓋未
登大寶而相與已素矣且
孝宗十載始
召諸臣面對其
召也雖内侍不及知夫
恭嘿思道是惟不言言乃雍
沉幾觀變是惟不行行乃果
宸衷獨發固不可測也今
===
上厲精圖治日臨羣臣益明習
國家事且將舉
祖
宗故典以備

保泰之道則愚何知焉
第二問
熊惟學

===
祖
宗故典以備
熙朝盛美蓋有待焉草莽愚生傾心拭目於是
舉也久矣若釋此而他求
保泰之道則愚何知焉
第二問
熊惟學
punctuated:
二祖諸臣皆從事乎草昧劬勩間，而宣德、弘治所親禮，乃其輔導之舊，蓋未登大寶而相與已素矣。且孝宗十載，始召諸臣面對；其召也，雖内侍不及知。夫恭嘿思道，是惟不言，言乃雍；沉幾觀變，是惟不行，行乃果。宸衷獨發，固不可測也。今上厲精圖治，日臨羣臣，益明習國家事，且將舉祖宗故典，以備熙朝盛美，蓋有待焉。草莽愚生傾心拭目於是舉也久矣。若釋此而他求保泰之道，則愚何知焉？

第二問
熊惟學
translation_en:
…the ministers of the two founding emperors all served amid the arduous labors of the dynasty’s beginnings, whereas those whom the Xuande and Hongzhi emperors treated with personal courtesy were their former tutors and advisers. Their association had thus long preceded their accession to the throne. Moreover, only in the tenth year of his reign did Emperor Xiaozong summon the ministers for a face-to-face audience; even the palace attendants had no advance knowledge of the summons. Reverently silent, he pondered the Way: he might refrain from speaking, but when he spoke, his words were harmonious. Delving deeply into the incipient workings of affairs, he observed changes: he might refrain from acting, but when he acted, he was resolute. Decisions issuing solely from the imperial mind were indeed beyond anyone’s fathoming.

The present emperor devotes his energies to achieving good government, receives his ministers daily, and grows ever more thoroughly acquainted with affairs of state. He also intends to revive the established precedents of his imperial ancestors, bringing the glories of this flourishing reign to their fullness. There is thus something still to await. I, an ignorant scholar among the common people, have long set my heart on this undertaking and eagerly watched for it. If one abandons this and seeks elsewhere a way to preserve peace and prosperity, what could I possibly know of such a course?

Second Policy Question
Xiong Weixue

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
同考試官署郎中袁批法制沿革之辨議者紛紛此
作揔衆論訂是非深切肯綮可假使荀卿復生亦當心服
同考試官都給事中宋批修復舊法以責實效非識時
務者不能道敬服
同考試官編修趙批指陳四弊究法壅窒之故
深為明切是庸心於世務者
同考試官修撰羅批四弊去則法行確論也
考試官學士吕批指陳時事深中弊源蓋留心世
故者□敬
===
考試官大學士張批識時務者謂之俊傑于其人然
法不可以輕變也亦不可以苟因也苟因
則承敝襲舛有頹靡不振之虞此不事事
之過也輕變則厭故喜新有更張無序之
患此泰多事之過也二者法之所禁也而
且犯之又何暇責其能行法哉去二者之
過而一求諸實法斯行矣執事發策考荀
孟之異論稽
國家之舊章審沿革之所宜求綜覈之實效

同考試官都給事中宋　批〔修復舊法以責實效非識時務者不能道斯邪〕
同考試官編修趙　批〔指陳四弊究法塞室之故深爲明切是庸心於世務者〕
同考試官修撰羅　批〔四弊去則法行確論也〕
考試官學士呂　批〔指陳時事深中弊源蓋留心世故者歟〕
考試官大學士張　批〔識時務者謂之俊傑予其人歟〕
===
法不可以輕變也不可以苟因也苟因
則承敝襲舛有頹靡不振之虞此不事事
之過也輕變則厭故喜新有更張無序之
患此泰多事之過也二者法之所禁也而
且犯之又何暇責其能行法哉去二者之
過而一求諸實法斯行矣執事發策考苟
孟之異論稽
國家之舊章審沿革之所宜求綜覈之實效
punctuated:
同考試官署郎中袁批：法制沿革之辨，議者紛紛。此作揔衆論，訂是非，深切肯綮。可假使荀卿復生，亦當心服。

同考試官都給事中宋批：修復舊法以責實效，非識時務者不能道。敬服。

同考試官編修趙批：指陳四弊，究法壅窒之故，深為明切，是庸心於世務者。

同考試官修撰羅批：四弊去則法行，確論也。

考試官學士吕批：指陳時事，深中弊源，蓋留心世故者。□敬。

考試官大學士張批：識時務者謂之俊傑，于其人然。

法不可以輕變也，亦不可以苟因也。苟因則承敝襲舛，有頹靡不振之虞，此不事事之過也。輕變則厭故喜新，有更張無序之患，此泰多事之過也。二者法之所禁也，而且犯之，又何暇責其能行法哉？去二者之過，而一求諸實，法斯行矣。執事發策，考荀孟之異論，稽國家之舊章，審沿革之所宜，求綜覈之實效。
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Yuan, Acting Director, comments: Opinions abound in the debate over retaining or changing laws and institutions. This essay brings together the various arguments and determines what is right and wrong, penetrating to the heart of the matter. If [?] Master Xun were to return to life, even he would surely be convinced.

Associate Examiner Song, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: To restore the old laws and demand practical results—only someone who understands the needs of the times could say this. I respectfully admire it.

Associate Examiner Zhao, Hanlin Compiler, comments: The essay identifies four abuses and investigates why implementation of the laws is obstructed. It is incisive and lucid; its author is someone who devotes thought to public affairs.

Associate Examiner Luo, Hanlin Senior Compiler, comments: Once the four abuses are removed, the laws will be implemented. This is a sound judgment.

Examiner Lü, Academician, comments: In addressing current affairs, the essay strikes directly at the sources of abuse. Its author evidently pays close attention to worldly affairs. [Illegible] respect [?].

Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: Those who understand the needs of the times are called outstanding talents. This is true of this man.

Laws must neither be changed lightly nor retained unthinkingly. Unthinking retention perpetuates defects and repeats errors, risking decline and stagnation: this is the fault of neglecting one's duties. Rash change means disliking the old and delighting in the new, risking disorderly alterations: this is the fault of excessive meddling. Both are forbidden by the laws. If someone nevertheless commits these faults, how can one even begin to demand that he be capable of implementing the laws? Eliminate these two faults and seek practical substance alone, and the laws will then be implemented. You, honored examiners, have posed a policy question examining the differing arguments of Xunzi and Mencius, investigating the established institutions of our state, weighing what should appropriately be retained or changed, and seeking practical results through comprehensive scrutiny…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
愚嘗伏而思之夫法制無常近民爲要古
今異勢便俗爲宜孟子曰遵先王之法而
過者未之有也此欲法先王矣荀卿曰略
先王而足亂世術不知法後王而一制度
是俗儒者也此欲法後王矣兩者互異而
荀爲近焉何也法無古今惟其時之所宜
與民之所安耳時宜之民安之雖庸衆之
所建立不可廢也戾於時拂於民雖聖哲
之所創造可無從也後王之法其民之耳
===
而目之也久矣久則有司之籍詳而衆人
之智熟道之而易從令之而易喻故曰法
後王便也往代無論已
明興
高皇帝神聖統天經緯往制博稽逖采靡善弗
登若六卿倣夏公孤紹周型漢祖之規摹
憲唐宗之律令儀有宋之家法采勝國之
曆元而隨時制宜因民立政取之近代者
十九稽之往古者十一又非徒然也即如

明興

登若六卿倣夏公孫紹周型漢祖之規摹
憲唐宗之律令儀有采之家法采勝國之
曆元而隨時制宜因民立政取之近代者
十九稽之往古者十一又非徒然也即如
punctuated:
愚嘗伏而思之：夫法制無常，近民爲要；古今異勢，便俗爲宜。孟子曰：「遵先王之法而過者，未之有也。」此欲法先王矣。荀卿曰：「略先王而足亂世術，不知法後王而一制度，是俗儒者也。」此欲法後王矣。兩者互異，而荀爲近焉。何也？法無古今，惟其時之所宜與民之所安耳。時宜之，民安之，雖庸衆之所建立，不可廢也；戾於時，拂於民，雖聖哲之所創造，可無從也。後王之法，其民之耳而目之也久矣。久則有司之籍詳，而衆人之智熟，道之而易從，令之而易喻。故曰：法後王便也。往代無論已。
明興，高皇帝神聖統天，經緯往制，博稽逖采，靡善弗登。若六卿倣夏，公孤紹周，型漢祖之規摹，憲唐宗之律令，儀有宋之家法，采勝國之曆元，而隨時制宜，因民立政。取之近代者十九，稽之往古者十一，又非徒然也。即如
translation_en:
I have humbly reflected upon this: laws and institutions have no fixed form; what matters is that they accord with the people. Circumstances differ between antiquity and the present; what is appropriate is to accommodate prevailing customs. Mengzi said: “There has never been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and went astray.” This advocates taking the former kings as models. Xun Qing said: “Those who give scant attention to the former kings and content themselves with the techniques of a disordered age [?], failing to understand how to model themselves on the later kings and unify institutions, are vulgar scholars.” This advocates taking the later kings as models. The two positions differ, but Xun’s comes closer to the mark. Why? Laws are neither inherently ancient nor inherently modern: all that matters is their suitability to the times and the people’s ease with them. If they suit the times and the people are at ease with them, they must not be discarded, even if ordinary men established them. If they run counter to the times and offend the people, they need not be followed, even if sages devised them. The people have long heard and seen the laws of the later kings. With time, the responsible officials’ records become detailed, and the people become thoroughly familiar with them. When guided, they readily follow; when given orders, they readily understand. Thus I say that taking the later kings as models is expedient. Let us leave earlier dynasties aside.
When the Ming arose, Emperor Gao, in his divine sagacity, exercised Heaven’s sovereign authority. He wove together earlier institutions, examining widely and drawing from distant sources, admitting every good practice. Thus the Six Ministers followed the Xia, and the Three Dukes and Three Junior Dukes continued the Zhou institutions. He modeled his arrangements on those of the Han founder, took the statutes and ordinances of the Tang ancestral emperor as his standard, followed the Song imperial house’s established rules, and adopted the calendrical epoch of the preceding dynasty. Yet he adapted these to the needs of the times and established government in accordance with the people. Nine tenths were drawn from recent dynasties, and one tenth was based on distant antiquity; this, too, was not without reason. For example, …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
算商賈置鹽官則桑孔之遺意也論停解
制年格則崔亮之選除也兩稅三限則楊
炎之田賦也保甲戶馬經義取士則安石
之新法也諸如此類未可悉數固前代所
謂陋習敝政也而今皆用之反以收富疆
之效而建昇平之業故善用之則庸衆之
法可使與聖哲同功而況出於聖哲者乎
故善法後王者莫如
高皇帝矣
===
天府之所藏掌故習之郡國之所頒有司守
之大小相維鴻纖具備自三代以來法制
之善未有過於
昭代者也然今甫二百餘年耳科條雖具而
美意漸荒申令雖勤而實效罔獲屯田興
矣土曠猶故也鹺政舉矣蜚輓猶故也清
勾數矣乏伍猶故也積粟課矣空廩猶故
也豈法之敝而不可行哉故議者謂宜有
所更張而後可以新天下之耳目者愚竊

punctuated:
算商賈、置鹽官，則桑孔之遺意也；論停解、制年格，則崔亮之選除也；兩稅三限，則楊炎之田賦也；保甲、戶馬、經義取士，則安石之新法也。諸如此類，未可悉數，固前代所謂陋習敝政也，而今皆用之，反以收富疆之效，而建昇平之業。故善用之，則庸衆之法可使與聖哲同功，而況出於聖哲者乎？故善法後王者，莫如高皇帝矣。
天府之所藏，掌故習之；郡國之所頒，有司守之。大小相維，鴻纖具備。自三代以來，法制之善，未有過於昭代者也。然今甫二百餘年耳，科條雖具，而美意漸荒；申令雖勤，而實效罔獲。屯田興矣，土曠猶故也；鹺政舉矣，蜚輓猶故也；清勾數矣，乏伍猶故也；積粟課矣，空廩猶故也。豈法之敝而不可行哉？故議者謂宜有所更張，而後可以新天下之耳目者，愚竊
translation_en:
…taxing merchants and establishing salt officials perpetuated the ideas of Sang and Kong; provisions concerning suspension and discharge [?], and the establishment of seniority rules, followed Cui Liang’s methods of selecting and appointing officials. The two taxes and three payment deadlines followed Yang Yan’s land taxation; the baojia household organization, household horse-keeping, and selection of officials through interpretations of the Classics followed Anshi’s New Policies. Such examples are too numerous to enumerate. These were precisely what earlier ages called pernicious practices and defective policies. Yet today they are all employed, and have instead brought wealth and strength and established an era of peace. Thus, when used well, even the institutions of ordinary men can achieve results equal to those of sages—how much more those originating with sages themselves! Hence none surpassed Emperor Gao in skillfully taking the later kings as his models.
What is preserved in the imperial archives, the officials responsible for precedents learn; what is promulgated throughout the provinces, the responsible authorities observe. Great and small sustain one another, and everything, from the broadest provisions to the finest details, is fully supplied. Since the Three Dynasties, no age has surpassed our illustrious dynasty in the excellence of its laws and institutions. Yet now barely two hundred years have passed. Although the regulations remain complete, their fine intentions have gradually been neglected; although commands are repeatedly issued, practical results are not obtained. Agricultural colonies have been established, yet land lies waste as before. The salt administration has been put into operation, yet the burden of urgent grain transport remains as before. Audits and the tracing of men liable for military service are frequent, yet the ranks remain depleted as before. Grain accumulation is required, yet the granaries remain empty as before. Can it be that the institutions are defective and cannot be implemented? Thus, regarding those who argue that changes must be made before the realm can be presented with something new to see and hear, I humbly venture …

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
以爲不然也夫
高皇帝之始爲法也
律令三易而後成官制晚年而始定一時名
臣英佐相與持籌而算之其利害審矣後
雖有智巧蔑以踰之矣且以
高皇帝之聖哲猶俯循庸衆之所爲乃以今之
庸衆而欲易
聖哲之所建豈不悖乎車之不前也馬不力也
不策馬而策車何益法之不行也人不力
也不議人而議法何益下流壅則上溢上
源窒則下枯决其壅疏其窒而法行矣今
之爲法壅者其病有四愚請頌言而毋諱
可乎夫天下之治始乎嚴常卒乎弛而人
之情始乎奮常卒乎怠今固已怠矣幹蠱
之道如塞漏舟而今且泄泄然以爲毋擾
耳一令下曰何煩苛也一事興曰何操切
也相與務爲無所事事之老成而崇尚夫
坐嘯畫諾之惇大以此求理不亦難乎此

以爲不然也。夫高皇帝之始爲法也，律令三易而後成，官制晚年而始定。一時名臣英佐，相與持籌而算之，其利害審矣，後雖有智巧，蔑以踰之矣。且以高皇帝之聖哲，猶俯循庸衆之所爲，乃以今之庸衆而欲易聖哲之所建，豈不悖乎？車之不前也，馬不力也；不策馬而策車，何益？法之不行也，人不力也；不議人而議法，何益？下流壅則上溢，上源窒則下枯；决其壅，疏其窒，而法行矣。

translation_en:
…I believe this is not so. When Emperor Gao first established the laws, the statutes and ordinances underwent three revisions before reaching completion, and the system of official posts was not settled until his later years. The eminent ministers and outstanding aides of that time deliberated together, calculating with counting rods; they thoroughly examined the benefits and harms. Even clever and resourceful men in later times could not surpass them. Moreover, even Emperor Gao, with his sagely wisdom, condescended to follow the practices of ordinary people. Yet ordinary people today wish to alter what a sage established. Is this not perverse? When a carriage fails to advance, it is because the horses do not exert themselves. What use is whipping the carriage instead of the horses? When laws are not implemented, it is because people do not exert themselves. What use is finding fault with the laws instead of the people? When the lower reaches are obstructed, water overflows upstream; when the source is blocked, the lower reaches dry up. Clear the obstructions and open the blockages, and the laws will operate.
There are four maladies that now obstruct the operation of the laws. May I, in my humble judgment, speak openly of them without concealment? The government of the realm begins with strictness but commonly ends in laxity; human endeavor begins with energy but commonly ends in indolence. Today we have certainly reached indolence. Remedying decay is like plugging a leaking boat, yet people now remain complacent, thinking only that they should avoid causing disturbance. Whenever an order is issued, they say, “How vexatious and harsh!” Whenever an undertaking is launched, they say, “How coercive and hasty!” Together they strive to display the seasoned maturity of men who do nothing at all, and esteem as generosity and broad-mindedness the conduct of those who sit whistling and merely sign their approval. Is it not difficult to seek good government in this way? This…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
病在積習者一也天下之勢上常重而下
常輕則運之為易今法之所行常在於卑
寡勢之所阻常在於衆疆下挾其衆而威
乎上上恐見議而畏乎下陵替之風漸成
指臂之勢難使此病在紀綱者二也夫多
指亂視多言亂聽言貴定也今或一事未
建而論者盈庭一利未興而議者踵至是
以任事者多却顧之虞而善宦者工遁藏
之術此病在議論者三也夫屢省考成所
===
以興事也故采其名必稽其實作於始必
考其終則人無隱忠而事可底績今一制
之立若曰著為令矣曾不崇朝而遽聞停
罷一令之施若曰布海内矣而畿輔之内
且格不行利害不究其歸而賞罰莫必其
後此病在名實者四也四者之弊熟於人
之耳目而入於人之心志非一日矣今不
祛四者之弊以决其壅疏其窒而欲法之
行雖日更制而月易令何益乎夫漢宣帝

且格不行利害不究其歸而賞罰莫必其

祛四者之弊以决其壅蹶其窒而欲法之
行雖日更制而月易令何益乎夫漢宣帝
punctuated: 病在積習者，一也。天下之勢，上常重而下常輕，則運之為易。今法之所行，常在於卑寡；勢之所阻，常在於衆疆。下挾其衆而威乎上，上恐見議而畏乎下。陵替之風漸成，指臂之勢難使。此病在紀綱者，二也。夫多指亂視，多言亂聽，言貴定也。今或一事未建，而論者盈庭；一利未興，而議者踵至。是以任事者多却顧之虞，而善宦者工遁藏之術。此病在議論者，三也。夫屢省考成，所以興事也。故采其名，必稽其實；作於始，必考其終。則人無隱忠，而事可底績。今一制之立，若曰著為令矣，曾不崇朝而遽聞停罷；一令之施，若曰布海内矣，而畿輔之内且格不行。利害不究其歸，而賞罰莫必其後。此病在名實者，四也。四者之弊，熟於人之耳目，而入於人之心志，非一日矣。今不祛四者之弊，以决其壅、疏其窒，而欲法之行，雖日更制而月易令，何益乎？夫漢宣帝
translation_en:
…the first is a failing rooted in entrenched habits. In the balance of power within the realm, when those above consistently carry greater weight and those below less, directing affairs is easy. Today, laws are generally enforced against the lowly and those with few supporters, while resistance comes from the numerous and powerful. Those below rely on their numbers to intimidate those above; those above fear criticism and stand in dread of those below. A tendency to undermine authority gradually takes hold, and the hierarchy can no longer function like an arm directing its fingers. This is the second failing, rooted in the governing order.

Many pointing fingers confuse the sight; many voices confuse the hearing. What matters in counsel is reaching a settled judgment. Today, before a single undertaking has been established, critics fill the court; before a single benefit has been secured, disputants arrive one after another. Thus those who undertake responsibility are beset by anxious backward glances, while those adept at official careers perfect the arts of evasion and concealment. This is the third failing, rooted in deliberation.

Repeated inspection and assessment of accomplishments are the means of advancing affairs. Thus, when accepting a reported claim, one must verify its substance; when something is undertaken at the outset, one must assess its outcome. Then no one will withhold loyal service, and undertakings can achieve results. Today, when a regulation is established, it is as though one were to say, “It has been set down as an ordinance!” Yet before a morning has passed, word suddenly comes that it has been suspended. When an ordinance is put into effect, it is as though one were to say, “It has been promulgated throughout the realm!” Yet even within the metropolitan region it is obstructed and not enforced. Benefits and harms are not investigated through to their ultimate effects, and rewards and punishments cannot be counted on to follow. This is the fourth failing, rooted in the discrepancy between name and reality.

The evils of these four failings have long been familiar to people’s eyes and ears and have penetrated their hearts and minds. If we now seek to have the laws enforced without first removing these four evils, breaking through their obstructions and clearing their blockages, what benefit would there be even in changing regulations every day and ordinances every month? Now Emperor Xuan of the Han…

title: 隆慶五年會試錄
text:
綜覈之主也然考其當時所行則固未嘗
新一令創一制惟曰取其祖宗之法修飭
而振舉之如曰漢家自有制度耳且其所
任魏相最為稱上意者亦未嘗以已意有
所論建惟條奏漢家故事及名臣賈誼晁
錯等言耳當其時雖五日一視事而上下
相維無苟且之意吏不奉宣詔書則有責
上計簿徒具文則有責三公不察吏治則
有責其所以振刷綜理者皆未嘗少越於
===
舊法之外惟其實事求是而不采虛聲信
賞必罰而真偽無眩是以當時吏稱其職
民安其業政事文學法理之士咸精其能
下至技巧工匠後世鮮及故崔寔稱其優
於孝文而仲長統極其嘆服荀悅論美元
帝而李德裕深以為非良不誣矣然則今
之欲求治理者又奚以紛紛多事為哉
高皇帝畢智竭慮以定一代之制非如漢祖之
日不暇給也
